### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

This paper establishes, using the best available national PBF policy data (InformEd States, 2003–2020), the full IPEDS census of public institutions, and current staggered-adoption estimators (Sun–Abraham with never-treated controls, Gardner two-stage, TWFE), that state PBF systems — including those with workforce/ROI premiums and those tying 10% or more of funding to performance — were not followed by large, robust shifts in completions by broad field or credential type through 2020. That pattern-level conclusion is consistent across many outcomes, estimators, and sample restrictions; it sits comfortably with the broader PBF null literature; and it is worth citing at that altitude, along with Tables 1–2, whose state-by-year coding of funded PBF, workforce premiums, and high-dosage status is a durable public good. The field should weigh the paper's stronger claims much more lightly. The null is judged under Bonferroni-adjusted 99.72%/99.85% intervals (the figure notes misprint the latter as 99.99%), the paper reports no coefficient, standard error, or interval bound anywhere, the 9%/11% minimum detectable effects are computed with institution-level standard errors while the models cluster by state and apply only to aggregate outcomes, a treatment that switches on and off in many states is run through absorbing-cohort estimators (attenuating toward zero), the 'workforce PBF' indicator bundles field premiums with earnings metrics and is compared against never-PBF states rather than PBF-without-premium states, and several outcomes show converging pre-trends the text mentions only in passing. Field × credential × race cells with baseline means of 2–4 awards per institution cannot support evidence-of-absence claims, so the Discussion's 'substantively' null language, its 'encouraging' reading of the racially minoritized student results, its claim that ROI-focused PBF removed the certificate-shifting incentive, and its recommendation of upfront funding all outrun the exhibits. Read it as a credible failure to find large effects of modest-dosage PBF designs over short horizons — not as evidence that field-targeted incentives do nothing, and not as a refutation of Li (2020) — and re-derive any number from the tables before quoting it, because the balance paragraph and the sample counts in the text do not match the tables.

#### Key Strengths

- Best available policy measurement paired with a population panel: the InformEd States database distinguishes funded from enacted PBF and codes workforce premiums and dosage year by year, and the full state-by-year treatment coding is printed in Tables 1–2, so the treatment side of the study is auditable without any restricted data.
- Current, correctly motivated estimator suite — Sun–Abraham with never-treated comparisons as the main specification, Gardner did2s and TWFE as alternatives — plus an unusually broad robustness program (no-controls, non-abandoning treatment group, PBF-without-feature comparison group, relaxed alpha, alternative Carnegie splits; roughly 36 appendix figures).
- A genuinely new outcome margin: completions decomposed by CIP-2 field within bachelor's, associate, and short/long certificates, overall and for racially minoritized students, at national scale in both sectors. This directly tests the reallocation channel that aggregate PBF nulls could not, and targets the two design features (workforce/ROI metrics, high dosage) that characterize contemporary PBF.
- Candid self-assessment where it counts: the Limitations section names the mechanism black box, the CIP-2 mismatch with state formulas, pre-trend violations for specific outcomes, and thin post-periods for high-dosage adopters; MDEs are reported at all; and the paper confronts Li (2020) and the Hillman certificate findings by name rather than ignoring them.
- The Discussion's dosage arithmetic (Michigan's STEM metric inside a <2% system; Pennsylvania's 4%; Texas's 2 of 12 points) gives readers a concrete, mechanically plausible reason the incentives were too small to move field composition.

#### Key Concerns

- Precision — the only thing that makes a null informative — is neither reported nor verifiable: no point estimates, standard errors, CI bounds, or per-regression Ns appear anywhere; the entire evidentiary base is five dense coefficient plots plus unlinked supplemental figures; there is no data availability statement, replication package, or code; and the zero-handling rule for logged counts and the cohort-assignment rule for on/off treatment are unstated.
- The inference design mechanically favors the null and the stated power does not describe the models estimated: Bonferroni-adjusted 99.72%/99.85% intervals (misprinted as 99.99% in the Figure 2–3 notes) are used in every main figure, while the 9%/11% MDEs are computed from institution-level robust SEs even though the regressions cluster by state and refer only to aggregate credential counts. For small fields, high-dosage PBF (about seven treated four-year states, 69 institutions), and the RM subgroup, intervals are consistent with effects of 30–50% or more in either direction.
- Treatment construction limits what the design-feature questions can answer: PBF switches on and off in Kansas, Florida, Arizona, Minnesota, Oregon and others but is fed to absorbing-cohort estimators (attenuating toward zero); 'workforce PBF' pools field-completion premiums with earnings/employment metrics; the main comparison for both design features is never-PBF states rather than PBF-without-feature states; and in the four-year sector nearly every PBF state has a workforce premium, so 'any PBF' and 'workforce PBF' are near-collinear. Several controls (state appropriations per FTE, enrollment, tuition, aid) are plausibly post-treatment.
- Text–table disagreements that survived production: the balance paragraph misstates RM completion shares (Tables 4–5 give 15.6–20.8% four-year and 17.9–27.2% two-year, not '15–17%' and '17–20%'), the bachelor's-degree gap (52.47, not 'less than 50'), and the direction of population differences in the two-year sector; sample counts do not reconcile (446 used for both the full four-year sample and the treated group; Table 4 sums to 433; text says 626 two-year adopters vs. Table 5's 614; 168 + 614 = 782, not 807); Table 5's short- plus long-term certificates exceed the certificate total in every column; Table 7 prints '8,379,70.43'; a Results cross-reference points to the wrong appendix figure; Equation 1 is typeset inconsistently and is the TWFE model rather than the estimator used.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** Not every column. The short- plus long-term certificate rows exceed the certificate total only in the four all-student columns, by 50 to 114; the subgroup columns add up. The same pattern appears in the working paper, so it sits in the variable construction; which cell is wrong cannot be settled from the public record. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered table.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** Partly withdrawn. Every table note says the descriptive statistics are for the base year (2003), and institutions in the 2003–2020 panel that are absent from the base year account for the gaps: 446 − 433 = 13 four-year institutions, and 807 − 782 = 25 two-year (12 of the 626 adopters and 13 of the 181 comparison institutions). The working paper's pre-exclusion 526/916 minus footnote 3's removals gives 447/807. So 446, 807 and 626 are consistent with the tables as panel totals, though the article never says so, and the MDE calculation, which uses the totals, is unaffected. What does not reconcile is p. 7's "27 states (446 institutions) adopted PBF": 446 is the whole four-year sample, and with 185 never-adopters in Table 4 the treated count must lie between 248 and 261. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered tables and the working paper.

- Rhetoric outruns the exhibits and prior-work reconciliation is one-sided: 'substantively' null claims, the 'encouraging' RM null (which sits unreconciled against the same team's Ortagus et al. 2023 finding of RM harm under high-dosage PBF), the untested certificate-incentive mechanism, and the upfront-funding recommendation are not supported by anything estimated here; the divergence from Li (2020) is attributed entirely to this paper's advantages without noting the bundled treatment, count-vs-share outcome, or stricter threshold; and the Hillman non-replication occurs in a sample that excludes Tennessee (both sectors) and Ohio (four-year), the very states Hillman et al. (2018) studied.

#### What to Rely On

- Through 2020, adoption of PBF (any, with workforce premium, or high-dosage) was not followed by large — roughly double-digit — increases in bachelor's completions in the large high-ROI fields (engineering, business, health, biology) at public four-year institutions. These are the tightest estimates in the paper (corrected half-widths of roughly 0.08–0.10 log points) and the null there is genuinely informative.
- At the pattern level, across credentials, broad fields, estimators, and sample restrictions, no robust positive effect of field-targeted PBF on completion counts emerged, and the one candidate signal (high-dosage PBF on health completions at doctoral universities) is reported by the authors not to survive alternative specifications. Cite this as 'no evidence of large effects of modest-dosage PBF designs over short horizons.'
- Tables 1 and 2: the state-by-year coding of funded PBF, workforce premiums, and high-dosage status for the four-year and two-year sectors, 2003–2020. Note the South Carolina 1998–2002 row falls outside the window and footnote 3's sector-specific exclusions mean the tables are not the analytic sample.
- The dosage-arithmetic explanation for the null — that STEM/workforce metrics were typically a small share of a small performance-funded share (Michigan <2%, Pennsylvania 4%, Texas 2 of 12 points) — is a plausible, well-documented mechanism, though it is illustrative rather than estimated.
- Non-replication of Li (2020)'s positive STEM-premium finding under heterogeneity-robust staggered-adoption estimators, a broader treatment construct, and a stricter inference threshold. Cite it as 'not confirmed under a stricter, differently constructed test,' not as a refutation.
- The paper's own careful statement of its contribution (p. 3): extending workforce-incentive evidence to credential and institution types, to high-ROI fields beyond STEM, to racially minoritized students, and to non-incentivized fields. Cite that version, not the literature-review 'gap' sentence that overstates what was unknown.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- The abstract's 'PBF policies did not have a significant impact on completion ... across fields of study' as evidence of no effect — significance was judged at 99.72%/99.85% confidence with no reported bounds, and for small fields, high-dosage PBF, and RM subgroups the intervals are consistent with large effects in either direction.
- The 'encouraging' conclusion that PBF does not harm racially minoritized students' completion — RM × field cells have baseline means of 2–4 awards per institution, the outcome is a logged count rather than a share or gap (the margin on which prior harm was documented), and the same team's Ortagus et al. (2023) found RM harm under high-dosage PBF in overlapping data.
- The 9% and 11% minimum detectable effects — computed with institution-level robust SEs while the models cluster by state, and applicable only to aggregate credential counts, not to any field-level result; the figures' interval widths are the honest precision statement.
- Any claim about the marginal effect of a workforce premium or of high dosage — the main-figure comparison group is never-PBF states, 'workforce PBF' bundles field premiums with earnings metrics, 'any' and 'workforce' PBF are near-collinear in the four-year sector, and the PBF-without-feature comparisons live in unlinked appendix figures with very few comparison states.
- High-dosage results specifically — roughly seven treated four-year states (69 institutions), adoption concentrated in 2017–2020 with few post-periods, the widest intervals in every figure, no small-cluster inference correction, and nothing to say about the very-high-dosage regimes (e.g., Texas's 95% community college formula) the Discussion invokes.
- Nulls for associate degrees in Education & Public Service, long-term certificates, and computer science certificates — these show converging pre-trends (coefficients rising monotonically from about −0.35 at k = −5 to zero), so a flat post-period could mask a negative effect rather than indicate none.
- 'ROI-focused PBF may have reduced or eliminated institutions' incentives for promoting certificate completion' — untested by any ROI-metric-specific contrast, and the sample excludes Tennessee, where Hillman et al. documented certificate shifting.
- 'Providing more financial resources to institutions upfront may be a more effective way to improve completion' — base appropriations are a covariate, never a treatment; no comparison of funding modalities is estimated and no causal citation is offered.
- The balance paragraph (pp. 7–8) and any sample size taken from the text — RM shares, the bachelor's-degree gap, and the population-composition claims misreport Tables 4–7, and 446/626/807 do not reconcile with the table Ns (433 and 782); use the tables and re-derive.

(2025) is a same-team companion paper on the same policy coding, not independent corroboration.

### Methods Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

A competently executed staggered difference-in-differences event study on a strong national panel (IPEDS + InformEd States PBF policy data, 2003–2020), using the Sun and Abraham (2021) heterogeneity-robust estimator with never-treated comparisons and a reasonable battery of alternative estimators and sample restrictions. The design is appropriate for the question, but because the paper's entire contribution is a set of null results, the load-bearing claims are precision claims — and those are the weakest part: the reported minimum detectable effect is computed with the wrong standard errors and applies only to aggregate outcomes, the multiple-comparisons adjustment inflates every interval to 99.72%/99.99%, no numeric coefficients or standard errors appear anywhere in the paper, and a genuinely non-absorbing treatment (states repeatedly switch PBF on and off) is fed into estimators built for absorbing treatment.

**Strengths:**

- Data and policy measurement are a real asset. The InformEd States PBF database distinguishes funded from merely legislated PBF and codes design features (workforce premium, dosage share) year by year at the state level, which is a substantial improvement over the binary 'has PBF' coding common in earlier work. Combining it with the full IPEDS census of public institutions means there is no sampling frame problem and no attrition in the usual sense.
- The estimator choice is current and correctly motivated. The authors explicitly cite Goodman-Bacon (2021), Baker et al. (2022), and Sun and Abraham (2021), use the interaction-weighted estimator with never-treated comparisons rather than a naive TWFE event study, and then show TWFE and Gardner (2022) did2s as alternatives. This is exactly the right response to the staggered-adoption literature and is a genuine methodological advance over the prior PBF studies (e.g., Li 2020) whose findings they contradict.
- The robustness program is broad and pre-committed in the text: no-controls specifications (A1–A5), two alternative estimators (A6–A15), treatment-group restriction to non-abandoning states and comparison-group restriction to PBF-without-the-feature states (A16–A25), a relaxed alpha of .01 (A26–A30), an alternative 2-year Carnegie split (A31–A34), and exclusion of 64 mixed baccalaureate/associate colleges (A35–A36). Few papers in this literature check this many margins.
- Excluding the 79 four-year and 109 two-year institutions in states with pre-2003, continuously-running PBF is the right call for identification (their event windows are unobservable), and footnote 3 reports a sensitivity check adding back the states that had PBF but not the specific premium.
- The Limitations section is unusually candid for a null-results paper: it names the unobserved-mechanism problem, the CIP-aggregation problem (states may incentivize narrow subfields the 2-digit codes cannot resolve), explicitly concedes that pre-treatment coefficients deviate from zero for some outcomes and that those estimates 'should be interpreted with considerable caution,' and flags the short post-periods for late and high-dosage adopters.
- The authors do not oversell the one apparent positive signal. High-dosage PBF on health completions at doctoral universities visibly trends up in Figure 4, and rather than headline it they report that it does not survive the restrictive treatment group or the alternative estimators.

**Weaknesses:**

- Non-absorbing treatment forced into absorbing-treatment estimators. Tables 1 and 2 show that PBF repeatedly switches on and off: Arizona 4-year is 2013–2014 and 2016–2017; Kansas 4-year is 2006–2009, 2013, 2015, 2019–2020; Florida is 2008 then 2013–2020. But Equation 1 defines PBF_{i,t+k} as an indicator for 'institution i adopted PBF k years before t' — event time is measured from first adoption, and Sun and Abraham's interaction-weighted estimator assigns cohorts by first treatment year and assumes treatment persists. Kansas is therefore treated as a 2006 cohort and coded 'treated' at k = 4…13 even though PBF was unfunded in 2010–2012, 2014, and 2016–2018. The paper acknowledges the treatment group is 'a mixture of states that maintained PBF and those who did not' but never reconciles this with the estimator's assumptions. The mechanical direction of this misclassification is attenuation toward zero — i.e., toward the paper's headline finding. The restriction to non-abandoning states is the single most important robustness check in the paper and it is in the appendix, described only as not changing conclusions, with no numbers shown.
- The workforce-PBF and high-dosage estimands do not isolate the design feature in the main specification. Every figure note states the comparison group as 'institutions in states that did not adopt PBF during the analytic period.' So the workforce-PBF coefficient is (PBF + workforce premium) vs. (no PBF at all), not the marginal contribution of the premium — yet the paper's conclusion is a claim about the marginal value of the design ('workforce-oriented PBF metrics are not particularly effective'). The feature-vs-no-feature comparison is relegated to appendix figures. Worse, for the 4-year sector that comparison is barely estimable: of the 27 PBF-adopting states in Table 1, only New Jersey, South Carolina (pre-period, excluded), and Vermont lack a workforce premium, and the first and last adopt only in 2020. Almost every PBF state has a workforce premium, so 'any PBF' and 'workforce PBF' are near-collinear treatments — which is visible in the figures, where the triangles and X markers overlap almost perfectly.
- The stated minimum detectable effect is not the MDE of the reported models. The paper computes the MDE as (z_{α/2} + z_β)·SE using 'robust standard errors at the institution level,' while every regression clusters at the state level. State clustering with strongly correlated within-state outcomes typically inflates SEs several-fold, so the true MDE is well above the reported 9% (4-year) and 11% (2-year). Reading half-widths off the figures makes this concrete: the tightest 'any PBF' bachelor's estimates (engineering, business, biology) have 99.72% half-widths of roughly 0.08–0.10 log points, implying an 80%-power MDE near 12%; but for high-dosage PBF on computer science bachelor's the k = +5 interval spans roughly −0.50 to +0.45, implying an MDE on the order of 50–60%. The MDE also refers to aggregate degree counts, not to the field-by-treatment-by-race cells that constitute nearly all the reported results.
- The multiple-comparisons correction mechanically manufactures the null. Bonferroni thresholds of α = .0028 (4-year) and α = .0015 (2-year) imply roughly 18 and 33 hypotheses, and produce 99.72% and 99.99% confidence intervals. A study whose contribution is 'we found no significant effects' has chosen the inference rule under which almost nothing could be significant. The authors cite Feise (2002) and Gelman et al. (2012) against Bonferroni and report α = .01 results in the appendix, but the main text, the abstract, and all five figures use the family-wise-corrected intervals. Note also that the correction is over outcomes, not over the roughly 500 event-time coefficients plotted per figure, so it is neither a genuine family-wise control over everything reported nor the conventional per-test rate.
- No numeric results appear anywhere. There is not a single point estimate, standard error, or p-value in the article — only five multi-panel coefficient plots at roughly 8 small panels each, plus 36 appendix figures. For a paper whose value rests entirely on how tightly zero is bounded, this is a serious transparency failure: readers cannot compute effect sizes, cannot assess precision quantitatively, cannot compare against Li (2020)'s STEM estimates, and cannot include the results in any meta-analysis. There is also no data-availability or open-practices statement.
- Zero-completion cells are never addressed. The outcome is the natural log of degree counts by 2-digit CIP field at the institution-year level. Many two-year colleges award zero engineering certificates or zero agriculture associate degrees in a given year — Table 5 shows certificate engineering with a mean of 13.0 and SD 28.6, which implies a large zero mass. The paper never states whether zeros are dropped, log(x+1)-transformed, or handled some other way. If dropped, the estimation sample is selected on the outcome and the selection margin (a program ceasing to award credentials) is precisely one channel through which PBF could operate. If log(x+1) or asinh, the coefficients are not log points and are sensitive to the units of the outcome (Chen and Roth, 2024). Either way the interpretation of the plotted coefficients as percentage changes is not established.
- Several controls are plausibly post-treatment. The covariate vector includes state appropriations per FTE, in-state tuition, instructional expenditure per FTE, grant aid, share receiving aid, and FTE enrollment. PBF is literally a mechanism for allocating state appropriations, so conditioning on appropriations per FTE conditions on a channel of the treatment; PBF is also documented in this literature to shift enrollment composition and institutional spending. Controlling for these attenuates estimates toward zero. The no-controls appendix figures (A1–A5) are described only as still supporting parallel trends — the text does not say whether the point estimates move.
- Baseline balance is overstated in the text. Table 7 shows the 2-year never-PBF comparison states have a Hispanic population averaging 510,481 versus 3,281,595 in PBF states (6.4×), an Asian population of 174,309 versus 979,129 (5.6×), and in-state tuition of \$3,645 versus \$2,651. Table 6 shows the 4-year high-dosage treated group at \$41,831 state income per capita versus \$50,087 for never-PBF, and an Asian population of 91,770 versus 997,823. The never-PBF comparison group is drawn from systematically smaller, and in the 4-year high-dosage case poorer, states. The claim that groups were 'well-balanced' and had 'similar racial/ethnic population compositions' rests on shares rather than the levels tabulated, and the levels matter for whether these states were on similar post-2008 higher-education trajectories.
- Pre-trend violations are more consequential than the text's phrasing suggests. Inspecting the figures, associate Education and Public Service (Figure 2) and long-term certificates (Figure 3) both show a clear monotone converging ramp: any-PBF coefficients near −0.35 at k = −5 rising steadily to zero at k = −1, then flat post-adoption. That is the canonical 'treated units were catching up' pattern. Relative to a counterfactual that extrapolates the pre-trend, a flat post-period is not a null — it is a negative effect. The text describes this only as 'a lack of support for the parallel trends assumption' and moves on. No formal pre-trend test, no Rambachan–Roth honest-DiD bounds, and no trend-adjusted specification is reported.
- Small-cluster inference is not addressed. Standard errors cluster at the state level, but Table 4 implies only about 7 treated states for 4-year high-dosage PBF (Florida, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Mississippi, Nevada, Oregon; N = 69 institutions) against roughly 23 never-adopting states. Cluster-robust asymptotics are unreliable with a treated-cluster count that small, and no wild cluster bootstrap or randomization inference is reported. This is exactly where the widest intervals and the one apparent positive result (doctoral health) both live.
- Sample sizes do not reconcile. The text reports 446 four-year and 807 two-year institutions in the sample, then says 27 states 'and 446 institutions' adopted PBF in the 4-year sector — the same 446 that is supposed to be the full sample including never-treated states. Table 4 sums to 433 four-year institutions (185 never-PBF + 248 any-PBF) at baseline and Table 5 to 782 two-year institutions (168 + 614, against 626 stated in the text). The MDE calculation then uses 446 and 807, i.e., the larger, apparently pre-exclusion figures. None of this is fatal, but a reader cannot tell what the estimation sample actually is.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** Partly withdrawn. Every table note says the descriptive statistics are for the base year (2003), and institutions in the 2003–2020 panel that are absent from the base year account for the gaps: 446 − 433 = 13 four-year institutions, and 807 − 782 = 25 two-year (12 of the 626 adopters and 13 of the 181 comparison institutions). The working paper's pre-exclusion 526/916 minus footnote 3's removals gives 447/807. So 446, 807 and 626 are consistent with the tables as panel totals, though the article never says so, and the MDE calculation, which uses the totals, is unaffected. What does not reconcile is p. 7's "27 states (446 institutions) adopted PBF": 446 is the whole four-year sample, and with 185 never-adopters in Table 4 the treated count must lie between 248 and 261. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered tables and the working paper.

- Event-time composition changes across k, and the paper does not flag it. The Sun–Abraham aggregate at each relative period is a cohort-share-weighted average of cohorts that are observed at that horizon. With data ending in 2020 and adoptions concentrated in 2013–2020, the k = 0 estimate draws on all cohorts while the k = +5 estimate is identified only from the earliest cohorts. The coefficient path across the x-axis is therefore not a within-cohort dynamic trajectory, and the noticeable widening of intervals at high k reflects both fewer clusters and different states, not just accumulating noise.
- Design–claim mismatch on the racial-equity question. The RM outcome is the logged count of credentials awarded to Black, Hispanic/Latino, and Native American students. The mechanism documented in the prior literature (Ortagus et al., 2023; Umbricht et al., 2017; Rosinger et al., 2023) is compositional — institutions substituting toward students who are cheaper to graduate. A null on the RM level, alongside a null on the total, is only weakly informative about that compositional claim; the paper never estimates the RM share of completions or a White–RM gap directly, which would be the outcome matching the hypothesis. RM counts are also smaller, zero-inflated, and visibly noisier in the figures than the all-student counts, so the RM intervals are the widest in the paper.
- Causal framing exceeds what the design delivers. The title says 'Impact,' the abstract says PBF 'did not have a significant impact,' and Equation 1's β_k is described as 'the treatment effect' — while elsewhere the paper says 'associated with' and the Discussion says PBF is 'not moving the needle.' Given the non-absorbing treatment, the acknowledged pre-trend violations, and the potentially post-treatment controls, these are state-policy-adoption contrasts, not clean impacts.
- Equation 1 as printed is the TWFE specification, not the estimator that produces the results. The paper presents the TWFE event-study equation as its model, defines β_k from it, and then explains that main estimates come from Sun and Abraham's interaction-weighted estimator instead. The typesetting of Equation 1 is also garbled (the outcome is written y_{i,t+l} in the text, and the k ≠ −1 exclusion is not visible), and the omitted-category and covariate-timing conventions for the interaction-weighted version are not spelled out.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Do not read this paper as evidence that PBF has no effect. Read it as: for the outcomes and horizons it can measure, effects large enough to clear a 99.72%/99.99% threshold are not detected. Those are different claims, and the gap between them is wide.
- Weight the results by which treatment and which outcome. The 'any PBF' estimates on large, common outcomes (total bachelor's, engineering, business, biology, health at four-year institutions) are the tightest in the paper — roughly ±8–10 log points at the corrected level — and those nulls are informative: they rule out double-digit effects. The 'high-dosage PBF' estimates, and anything involving small fields (computer science, agriculture, technical trades) or the RM subgroup, have intervals wide enough to be consistent with 30–50% effects in either direction. Citing the latter as null findings is not supportable.
- Do not use the reported 9% and 11% MDEs to characterize any specific result. They are computed with institution-level robust standard errors while the models cluster at the state level, and they refer to aggregate credential counts. If you need a precision statement for a particular field or subgroup, read the interval half-width off the relevant panel and back out the implied SE yourself — the paper reports no numbers you can use directly.
- Treat the workforce-premium results as 'PBF states versus non-PBF states' rather than 'premium versus no premium.' The main-specification comparison group is never-PBF states, and in the four-year sector almost every PBF state has a workforce premium, so 'any PBF' and 'workforce PBF' are nearly the same treatment on nearly the same states. If your question is whether adding a workforce metric to an existing PBF system changes anything, this paper's main figures do not answer it; the appendix figures that attempt to answer it have very few comparison states in the four-year sector.
- Discount the associate Education and Public Service, long-term certificate, and computer science certificate results entirely. The pre-treatment coefficients for the first two follow a clear monotone ramp from roughly −0.35 up to zero over k = −5 to −1. Under a counterfactual that respects that trend, a flat post-period would indicate a negative effect, not a null. The paper flags these as parallel-trends violations but still lists them among the null findings.
- The one live positive signal is high-dosage PBF on health completions at doctoral universities (Figure 4), which rises monotonically to roughly +0.25 to +0.30 log points by k = +5 with a flat pre-period. The authors report it does not survive their restrictive treatment group or their alternative estimators, and it is one of many hypotheses tested. Treat it as a hypothesis worth revisiting with more post-2020 data rather than as either an established effect or a settled false positive.
- Before citing the RM results as evidence that recent PBF does not harm minoritized students, note three things: the intervals are the widest in the paper; the outcome is a logged count with an unspecified number of zero cells, not a share or a gap; and the compositional mechanism documented in prior work would show up in shares, which this paper never estimates. The Discussion's characterization of these nulls as 'encouraging' is an evidence-of-absence claim the design does not deliver.
- If you are comparing this paper against Li (2020)'s positive STEM finding, the estimator upgrade is real and is a legitimate reason to prefer these estimates — but note that the divergence could equally reflect the different comparison group construction, the added controls (several of which are plausibly post-treatment), the log-count outcome and its zero handling, or the family-wise-corrected inference. The paper attributes the divergence to the methodological advance without testing which change drives it.
- If you plan to build on or extend this analysis, be aware that no coefficients, standard errors, or replication materials are provided. You will need to reconstruct the sample from IPEDS and the InformEd States database yourself, and the paper's own sample counts are internally inconsistent (446 versus 433 four-year; 626 versus 614 two-year treated) — so expect to have to make and document your own choices about the estimation sample.
- For policy audiences: the most defensible takeaway is narrow — modest-dosage PBF systems with workforce metrics adopted between 2003 and 2020, evaluated over horizons of at most five years and often fewer, did not produce large detectable shifts in the composition of credentials by field. The paper's own Discussion supplies the most likely reason (Michigan tied under 2% of state funds to PBF with STEM as one metric among many; Texas's 10% system gave 2 of 12 points to STEM), which means this is at least as much a null about incentive magnitude as about incentive design. It says essentially nothing about high-stakes regimes like Texas's newer 95%-performance community college formula.

**Detailed Commentary:**

This is a solid, conventional paper in the modern staggered-DiD idiom, and the identification strategy is a reasonable answer to the research question. Treatment is a state-level policy that turns on at different times in different states; the natural design is a staggered event study; the authors correctly recognize that TWFE is biased under treatment-effect heterogeneity and adopt Sun and Abraham (2021) with never-treated comparisons as their primary estimator, with Gardner (2022) two-stage DiD and TWFE as alternatives. Data are the population of relevant public institutions from IPEDS merged to the best available longitudinal PBF policy database, which distinguishes funded from merely enacted policy and codes design features year by year. Nothing about the basic architecture is wrong, and the paper is more careful than most of the PBF literature it is correcting.

What makes evaluating it difficult is that the paper is entirely a null-results paper, and null results are only as good as the precision behind them. Here the precision claims are the weakest part of the methods, in four compounding ways. First, the reported minimum detectable effects — 9% for four-year institutions, 11% for two-year — are computed from 'robust standard errors at the institution level,' while every reported regression clusters at the state level. Since PBF is a state-level treatment and institutional completions are strongly correlated within state, state clustering will inflate standard errors substantially, so the actual MDE of the estimated models is materially larger than the reported figure. Second, those MDEs describe aggregate degree counts, whereas essentially every result in the paper is a field-by-treatment or field-by-treatment-by-race cell with much smaller counts and higher variance; the paper notes this for 'smaller subfields such as computer science' but the headline precision statement is what readers will carry away. Third, the Bonferroni thresholds of α = .0028 and α = .0015 push every plotted interval to 99.72% and 99.99% coverage, which mechanically all but guarantees the paper's conclusion; the authors cite the standard critiques of Bonferroni and report α = .01 results in the appendix, yet the main text, the abstract, and all five figures use the conservative intervals. Fourth, no numeric estimates appear anywhere in the article, so no reader can independently assess how tight the nulls actually are without reading half-widths off small multi-panel plots. Doing that exercise shows the precision is highly uneven: the tightest 'any PBF' bachelor's-degree estimates have corrected half-widths around 0.08–0.10 log points, implying an MDE nearer 12% than 9% but still genuinely informative; the high-dosage estimates for small fields have intervals spanning nearly a full log point, which cannot distinguish a 40% decline from a 40% increase. The paper's uniform reporting of 'not statistically distinguishable from zero' flattens a real distinction between informative and uninformative nulls.

The most substantive design issue is that the treatment is not absorbing but is estimated as if it were. Tables 1 and 2 make this vivid: Arizona's four-year PBF runs 2013–2014 and again 2016–2017; Kansas runs 2006–2009, 2013, 2015, and 2019–2020; Minnesota, Michigan, Oregon, Illinois, and Massachusetts all have gaps. Equation 1 defines the event indicator relative to the year the institution 'adopted PBF,' and Sun and Abraham's interaction-weighted estimator partitions units into cohorts by first treatment year and constructs cohort-specific paths under the assumption that treatment persists. The paper acknowledges in one sentence that 'the treatment group consisted of a mixture of states that maintained PBF throughout the duration of the data period and those who did not,' but never explains how the estimator is reconciled with that fact. The direction of the resulting misclassification is clear — institution-years coded as treated but actually not under PBF dilute the estimated effect toward zero — and it therefore pushes in the same direction as the paper's headline conclusion. The robustness check that speaks directly to this, restricting the treatment group to non-abandoning states, exists in the appendix (Figures A16–A25) and is described in a single sentence as not materially changing the results. That check deserved to be in the main text with numbers, because it is the difference between a null and an artifact.

A second design issue concerns the estimand for the two policy-design features that give the paper its title. Every figure note states the comparison group as institutions in never-adopting states. So the workforce-PBF coefficient contrasts states with PBF-plus-workforce-premium against states with no PBF at all, and the high-dosage coefficient contrasts states with high-dosage PBF against states with no PBF at all. Neither isolates the marginal contribution of the design feature, which is what the paper's conclusions are about. The contrast that would isolate it — feature versus PBF-without-feature — is again in the appendix, and for the four-year sector it is close to inestimable: of the 27 PBF-adopting states in Table 1, only New Jersey and Vermont lack a workforce premium during the analytic period, and both adopt only in 2020 (South Carolina's 1998–2002 window falls outside). This near-universality of workforce premiums also means 'any PBF' and 'workforce PBF' are close to the same treatment applied to nearly the same states, which is why their markers overlap almost exactly in every panel. Readers should understand that RQ1's central design contrast has very little independent variation behind it in the four-year sector.

Outcome construction raises a question the paper never answers. The dependent variable is the natural log of the number of credentials awarded in a field at an institution in a year, and for many two-digit CIP fields at many institutions that count is zero — Table 5's certificate means (engineering 7.3 with SD 13.6, computer science 23.2 with SD 48.1) are consistent with a substantial zero mass. Whether zeros were dropped, transformed as log(x+1), or handled by asinh is not stated. If dropped, the estimation sample is conditioned on the outcome and the excluded observations are precisely the program-closure margin PBF might affect. If a shifted log or asinh is used, the coefficients are not interpretable as percentage changes and are sensitive to the outcome's units. Either way, the plotted coefficients cannot be read as clean elasticities without this information, and there is no data-availability or open-practices statement that would let a reader check.

On covariates: several of the included controls are plausibly affected by the treatment. State appropriations per FTE is the most obvious — PBF is a mechanism for allocating state appropriations, so conditioning on appropriations partially conditions away the treatment channel. FTE enrollment, in-state tuition, instructional expenditure per FTE, and financial aid receipt are also documented in this literature as PBF-responsive. Conditioning on post-treatment mediators biases estimates toward zero. The paper reports no-controls specifications in Appendix Figures A1–A5, but describes them only as continuing to support parallel trends; whether the point estimates change is not stated, and it is exactly what a reader would want to know.

Balance is overstated in the text. The narrative claim that groups were 'well-balanced' and that 'treatment and comparison states had similar racial/ethnic population compositions' sits uneasily with Table 7, where two-year never-PBF states average a Hispanic population of 510,481 against 3,281,595 in PBF states, an Asian population of 174,309 against 979,129, a White population of 3.9 million against 7.7 million, and in-state tuition of \$3,645 against \$2,651. In Table 6, the four-year high-dosage group averages \$41,831 in state income per capita against \$50,087 for never-PBF states. Shares may well be comparable even when levels are not, but the levels tell you the never-PBF comparison group is drawn from a systematically smaller and, for high-dosage, poorer set of states — which is directly relevant to whether their higher-education trajectories through the Great Recession and the subsequent enrollment decline would have tracked those of the treated states.

Pre-trends deserve more emphasis than the text gives them. The Limitations section concedes that 'for some analyses, pre-treatment coefficient estimates deviate from zero in at least one period.' Inspecting Figures 2 and 3 shows something more structured than an isolated deviation: for associate degrees in Education and Public Service, and for long-term certificates, the any-PBF coefficients climb monotonically from roughly −0.35 at k = −5 through −0.15, −0.10, −0.05 to zero at the omitted period, then sit flat near zero to slightly positive after adoption. That is a converging pre-trend, and relative to a counterfactual that extrapolates it, the flat post-period would represent a negative effect rather than a null. The paper offers no formal pre-trend test, no honest-DiD sensitivity bounds in the Rambachan–Roth sense, and no trend-adjusted specification, so a reader has no quantitative handle on how much the conclusion for these outcomes depends on the parallel-trends extrapolation.

Inference with few treated clusters is unaddressed. Standard errors cluster at the state level throughout, which is correct in principle, but for four-year high-dosage PBF there appear to be only about seven treated states (Florida, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Mississippi, Nevada, Oregon; Table 4 reports N = 69 institutions) against roughly 23 never-adopting states. Cluster-robust asymptotics are known to be unreliable at that cluster count, and neither a wild cluster bootstrap nor randomization inference is reported. Two of the paper's most-discussed results — the widest intervals, and the one apparently positive finding for high-dosage health completions at doctoral universities — both sit in exactly this thin-cluster region.

Finally, some reporting and framing issues that affect how much a reader can verify. Sample counts do not reconcile: the text reports 446 four-year and 807 two-year institutions in the sample, then reports that 27 states 'and 446 institutions' adopted PBF, which cannot both be true if there is a never-treated comparison group; Table 4 sums to 433 four-year and Table 5 to 782 two-year institutions; and the MDE calculation uses the larger 446 and 807 figures. Equation 1 is presented as the model but is the TWFE specification, not the interaction-weighted estimator that produces the headline results, and it is typeset with errors. Nothing numeric appears anywhere in the article. And the causal register is inconsistent — the title says 'Impact,' the abstract says PBF 'did not have a significant impact,' Equation 1's β_k is called 'the treatment effect,' but the purpose statement and much of the Discussion say 'associated with.' Given the non-absorbing treatment, the acknowledged pre-trend violations, and the arguably post-treatment controls, the more cautious language is the appropriate one.

On balance the paper is worth trusting for what it most defensibly shows: modest-dosage PBF systems with field-based premiums, over the horizons observable through 2020, did not produce large shifts in the field composition of credentials at public institutions, and the 'any PBF' nulls on large aggregate outcomes are tight enough to rule out double-digit effects. It should not be trusted as a general refutation of PBF design effects, as evidence that high-dosage PBF does nothing, or as evidence of absence of harm to racially minoritized students. The gap between those two readings is created less by any single error than by the accumulation of choices — an attenuating treatment coding, potentially post-treatment controls, family-wise-corrected intervals, and an understated MDE — that all push in the same direction as the conclusion.

My confidence is moderate rather than high. The methods narrative in the article is complete enough to assess the design, and reading the figures at high resolution let me verify pre-trend patterns and interval widths that the text characterizes only qualitatively. But 36 supplemental appendix figures carry every robustness check that matters most — the non-abandoning treatment group, the feature-versus-no-feature comparison groups, the alternative estimators, the no-controls specifications, and the relaxed-alpha results — and I could not see any of them. Nor does the paper report a single number I could check arithmetic against. Several of my sharper criticisms, particularly about the on-off treatment coding and the direction of attenuation, could be substantially blunted if those appendix figures show the restricted-treatment-group estimates are indistinguishable from the main ones with comparable precision.

---

### Literature Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper's coverage of the performance-based funding (PBF) literature is competent and current, and — unusually for a null-results paper — it explicitly names the two bodies of prior work its findings contradict (Li 2020 on STEM premiums; Hillman et al. 2015/2018 on certificate substitution) rather than burying them. But readers should know that the PBF evidence base it assembles is dominated by the authors' own research program and its InformEd States data, that its reconciliation with Li (2020) attributes the divergence to methodological superiority while omitting a substantive treatment-definition difference, and that the paper's core high-ROI/low-ROI field taxonomy rests partly on a non-peer-reviewed think-tank white paper. At least one citation is mischaracterized and one reference-list DOI is wrong.

**Strengths:**

- The paper directly confronts conflicting evidence instead of ignoring it. The discussion has a dedicated passage on why its results diverge from Li (2020), and a second on why its certificate findings diverge from Hillman et al. (2015, 2018) and Li & Ortagus (2019). Null-results papers frequently omit this; here a reader can see exactly which prior findings are in tension and reason about why.
- Coverage of the core PBF-effects corpus is genuinely broad and includes substantial work from outside the author group: Hillman, Tandberg & Gross (2014); Hillman, Tandberg & Fryar (2015); Hillman, Hicklin Fryar & Crespín-Trujillo (2018); Li (2017, 2020); Boland (2020, 2025); Chan, Mabel & Mbekeani (2023); Gándara & Rutherford (2020); Hagood (2019); Dougherty et al. (2014); and Shin et al. (2024). The claim of a null-to-modest consensus is not built only on in-group citations.
- The theoretical framing (principal–agent via Jensen & Meckling; gaming and selective attention via Franco-Santos & Otley 2018 and Taylor 2021) is used substantively rather than decoratively — the gaming mechanism is what generates the certificate-substitution prediction, and the resource-constraint mechanism (Hemelt et al. 2021 on why STEM/health credentials cost more to produce) is exactly the right citation for the paper's closing policy argument.
- The barriers-to-STEM section reaches sensibly across disciplines — economics (Li & Xia 2024 on grades and major choice; Bleemer et al. on major restrictions), psychology and sociology (Strayhorn; Murphy & Zirkel; Rainey et al. on belonging), and the pathways framing from Kizilcec et al. (2023, Science). For a policy-finance paper this is more interdisciplinary engagement than the genre usually offers.
- Descriptions of the Hillman studies are accurate. Hillman, Tandberg & Fryar (2015) is correctly characterized as finding short-term certificate increases without associate degree increases, and Hillman et al. (2018) is correctly used for the equal-weighting-of-credentials point. Readers can repeat these characterizations safely.

**Weaknesses:**

- The reconciliation with Li (2020) is asymmetric and incomplete. The paper attributes divergence entirely to its own advantages — 'more recent methodological advancements in difference-in-differences,' 'a more recent data source,' 'multiple sample restrictions' — i.e., three reasons why this paper should be believed over Li. It does not name the design differences that cut the other way. Most importantly, this paper's 'workforce PBF' treatment is a composite binary that pools STEM/health completion premiums with graduate employment and earnings metrics, whereas Li (2020) modeled STEM premiums specifically. Pooling a STEM premium with earnings metrics into one indicator mechanically dilutes a STEM-specific effect. There are also outcome and period differences (Li examined both the number and the share of STEM bachelor's degrees; this paper uses logged counts only, so the compositional-shift test that most directly matches the paper's own 'clustering students toward or away from fields' framing is absent). A reader who accepts the paper's account will conclude Li (2020) has been superseded, which is stronger than the evidence supports.
- The stated gap is overstated and internally inconsistent. The literature review closes with: 'To date, however, we do not have evidence of the extent to which field and ROI metrics in PBF models and policy dosage impact degree completion across different fields of study, especially among RM students and at non-4-year colleges.' The first clause is not true — Li (2020) is precisely evidence on field metrics and completion by field at public 4-year institutions, and the paper says so 200 lines earlier. The genuine novelty lives entirely in the 'especially' qualifiers plus dosage and fields beyond STEM. Two pages earlier the paper states the contribution correctly ('We extend the literature by examining how the effects of workforce-oriented incentives vary by credential or institution type, extend to high-ROI fields beyond STEM, and vary by student race/ethnicity'). Readers should cite the careful version, not the gap sentence.
- The closest antecedent is a same-team working paper whose overlap is never disclosed. Zahran et al. (2025), 'The impact of workforce-oriented performance-based funding on students' return on investment' (InformEd States working paper), shares five of six authors, the same InformEd States policy coding, and the same treatment construct. It appears exactly once, in a list of studies whose null findings this paper is 'in line with.' A reader encountering both should not treat them as independent confirmation — the agreement partly reflects a shared data pipeline and shared treatment definitions, not replication.
- Self-citation carries nearly all of the PBF-substantive load. Roughly a dozen of ~80 references are to the author group (Ortagus et al. 2020; the two 2023 Ortagus et al. papers; Rosinger et al. 2022, 2023; Kelchen et al. 2023; Kelchen 2018; Kelchen & Stedrak 2016; Li & Ortagus 2019; Umbricht, Fernandez & Ortagus 2017; the InformEd States dataset; Zahran et al. 2025), and they supply the framing claims about dosage thresholds, the policy landscape, the equity findings, and the treatment coding. This group has produced much of the recent PBF corpus, so the density is defensible — but it means the paper's picture of what PBF does is substantially one research program's picture, and the 10% high-dosage threshold in particular is a within-group convention rather than an externally validated cut point.
- One citation appears mischaracterized. Li (2017), 'Covet thy neighbor or reverse policy diffusion? State adoption of performance funding 2.0,' is a study of why states adopt PBF. It is cited at line 352 for the claim that 'Institutions then respond to PBF formulas by altering their programs and staffing to align with the specific policy goals' — an institutional-response claim the cited paper does not test. (The same source is used correctly later, for weak links between state characteristics and PBF adoption.) A reader should not repeat Li (2017) as evidence of institutional programmatic response.
- A load-bearing source is grey literature from an advocacy-oriented think tank. Cooper (2024), a FREOPP white paper, is cited six-plus times, including as one of three sources for the study's operational definition of high-ROI fields (STEM, business, health) versus low-ROI fields (education, humanities, arts), and as the sole source for two claims: that completion is 'a crucial first step for improving ROI,' and that sub-baccalaureate credentials 'yield higher returns on investment in high-demand fields compared to low-demand fields, regardless of degree level.' ROI calculations are highly sensitive to counterfactual-earnings assumptions, cost inputs, and discount rates, and this one has not been refereed. Bleemer et al. (2023) is likewise a Brookings commentary standing in for peer-reviewed work on major restrictions, and the Carnevale et al. Georgetown CEW reports supply the earnings-premium claims. The field taxonomy is at least triangulated against Andrews et al. (2024, REStat) and Zhang et al. (2024, AERJ); the single-source claims are not.
- Several intro/lit-review characterizations are loose enough to warrant verification. (a) 'On average, college degree holders earn more than those who complete a high school diploma or associate degree' — an associate degree is a college degree; the sentence conflates 'college degree' with 'bachelor's degree' in a paper whose whole point is credential-level heterogeneity. (b) 'RM students who earn a 4-year degree see higher individual rates of return than White students compared to high school graduates (Zhang et al., 2024)' — Zhang, Liu & Hu (2024) is titled and framed around internal rates of return by major using quantile regression; a headline racial comparison is a strong claim to hang on it. (c) 'discrepancy in access to high-earning majors among racial/ethnic groups plays a more significant role than access to different institutions (Bleemer et al., 2023)' — a strong comparative decomposition claim sourced to a blog post. (d) The bundling of Kelchen & Stedrak (2016) — which is about institutional financial priorities and aid allocation — into a sentence asserting that 'PBF negatively affects minoritized students' attributes more to that paper than it shows.
- Reference-list errors. Belfield & Bailey (2011), Community College Review 39(1), carries the DOI 10.1016/j.jfineco.2022.01.004 — which belongs to Baker, Larcker & Wang (2022) in the Journal of Financial Economics, the reference immediately above it in the list. Pierszalowski, Bouwma-Gearhart & Marlow (2021) is listed as Social Sciences 10(9), 334, but the DOI resolves to article 328. Belfield & Bailey (2017) and Dougherty et al. (2014) each have an unclosed parenthesis. These are copy-editing failures rather than substantive ones, but the Belfield & Bailey DOI will send a reader to the wrong paper entirely.
- The mechanisms and implementation literature on PBF is thin, which matters because the paper's contribution is an explanation of a null. Dougherty and colleagues' body of work on how PBF actually operates inside institutions — the ASHE report and the 2016 Johns Hopkins book on mechanisms and impacts — is represented only by a single 2014 CCRC working paper cited once for the cost of raising attainment. The paper cites essentially no qualitative work on PBF implementation, then in its own limitations section calls for exactly that ('Future research employing qualitative methods... could help illuminate the black box'). Some of that black box has already been opened.
- The paper does not connect its own detectable-effect floor to the size of the findings it says it contradicts. It reports a minimum detectable effect of roughly 9% for 4-year and 11% for 2-year outcomes at Bonferroni-adjusted alphas of .0028 and .0015 — a far stricter bar than the conventional .05 used by the studies it contrasts itself with. 'Our results diverged from previous research' is therefore a claim readers should not take at face value: a non-rejection under a 99.72% confidence interval with a 9% floor is compatible with a real effect of the magnitude Li (2020) reported. This is a statistical point, but it is a scholarly-positioning problem, because it determines whether the paper overturns prior work or merely fails to confirm it.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Do not read this paper as overturning Li (2020). Read them side by side and compare the treatment constructs first: Li modeled STEM premiums specifically; this paper's 'workforce PBF' indicator pools STEM/health completion premiums with graduate employment and earnings metrics, and its outcomes are logged counts rather than shares. Then compare Li's reported effect magnitudes against this paper's ~9% minimum detectable effect and its Bonferroni-adjusted 99.72% intervals. If Li's point estimates fall inside those intervals, the correct summary is 'not confirmed under a stricter test,' not 'contradicted.'
- Treat Zahran et al. (2025) — the InformEd States working paper on workforce-oriented PBF and student ROI — as a companion, not corroboration. Five of six authors overlap, and the policy coding is the same InformEd States dataset. If you are citing both for the proposition that workforce-oriented PBF does not work, say so as one research program's finding across two outcomes, not two independent studies.
- Verify before repeating: (a) the DOI for Belfield & Bailey (2011) in the reference list points to Baker, Larcker & Wang (2022) in the Journal of Financial Economics — look up the Community College Review article directly; (b) Li (2017) is a policy-diffusion study and does not support the institutional-response claim it is attached to on the theory page; (c) the racial-IRR claim attributed to Zhang, Liu & Hu (2024) and the majors-versus-institutions decomposition attributed to Bleemer et al. (2023) are both stronger than the cited sources' framing and should be checked at the source.
- Be cautious with the high-ROI/low-ROI field taxonomy. The STEM/business/health versus education/humanities/arts split is partly grounded in Cooper (2024), a FREOPP white paper that has not been peer reviewed. For peer-reviewed grounding go to Andrews, Imberman, Lovenheim & Stange (2024, Review of Economics and Statistics), Zhang, Liu & Hu (2024, AERJ), Webber (2016), and Eide, Hilmer & Showalter (2016) — all cited in the paper. Note that returns-to-major estimates vary substantially with selection controls, so the binary high/low framing is a modeling convenience, not a settled fact.
- For the PBF mechanisms this paper cannot observe, go to the implementation literature the paper mostly skips: Dougherty and colleagues' work on the mechanisms and impacts of performance funding (the ASHE report with Reddy, and the 2016 Johns Hopkins volume) documents what institutions actually did in response to PBF and why intended mechanisms often failed to fire. That literature is the natural complement to a paper whose central finding is a null attributed to insufficient dosage.
- For the paper's closing policy claim — that 'providing more financial resources to institutions upfront may be a more effective way to improve completion' — no causal evidence is cited. Deming & Walters' work on institutional spending and postsecondary attainment, and Bound and Turner's work on institutional resources and completion, are the standard causal sources for that proposition. Readers persuaded by the recommendation should get their evidence from there, not from this paper.
- Worth checking for yourself whether these PBF studies belong in your reading list, since they are absent here and I could not verify them against the text: Rutherford & Rabovsky (2014, ANNALS) on performance funding and student outcomes; Tandberg & Hillman (2014, Journal of Education Finance) on performance funding outcomes; Gándara & Rutherford's work on equity premiums and bachelor's degree production (distinct from the 2020 Educational Researcher access paper that is cited); Bell, Fryar & Hillman's meta-analysis of PBF research; and Ward & Ost on large-scale PBF in Ohio. Each is plausibly relevant to a paper claiming its null is consistent with the field consensus, and I flag them as leads rather than as confirmed omissions.
- When citing this paper, cite it for what it actually establishes: that under a stringent multiple-comparison-corrected event-study design using 2003–2020 InformEd States data, workforce-oriented and high-dosage PBF show no detectable effects on completion counts by broad CIP field, across credential levels, institution types, and for racially minoritized students. That is a real and useful extension beyond Li (2020) — particularly the 2-year sector, the non-STEM high-ROI fields, the dosage dimension, and the RM subgroup. Do not cite it for the proposition that field-based PBF incentives have been shown not to work.

**Detailed Commentary:**

**Where this paper sits.** This is the sixth or seventh output of the InformEd States PBF research program (Ortagus, Rosinger, Kelchen and collaborators), which over the past five years has become the field's dominant supplier of both PBF policy data and PBF effect estimates. That matters for how a reader should weigh it. The paper's core claim — workforce-oriented and high-dosage PBF do not move completion by field — is offered as consistent with 'previous null findings,' but the studies it is consistent with are disproportionately the group's own (Ortagus et al. 2020 synthesis; the two Ortagus et al. 2023 papers; Rosinger et al. 2022, 2023; Zahran et al. 2025), and the treatment coding across all of them comes from a single dataset the group built. The exception — the one genuinely independent finding on the exact question this paper asks — is Li (2020), and that finding points the other way. So the honest reader's summary is not 'yet another confirmation' but 'a stringent test from the dominant research program that fails to replicate the one prior positive finding, using a differently constructed treatment variable.'

**The Li (2020) reconciliation is the paper's most consequential positioning move, and it is one-sided.** Three reasons are given for the divergence, and all three are reasons to prefer this study: newer difference-in-differences estimators robust to staggered adoption and heterogeneous effects, newer PBF data covering 2003–2020, and multiple sample restrictions as robustness checks. Each is legitimate on its own terms. But the differences that cut the other way go unmentioned. The most important is the treatment construct. This paper's second treatment variable 'indicated whether a state's PBF system included a workforce-oriented performance premium,' defined to cover 'a range of PBF metrics that reward workforce-oriented outcomes, including completion in fields of study designated as being in high-demand or providing high-ROI, such as STEM and health, or metrics that account for graduates' employment or earnings.' That is a union of at least three distinct policy instruments. Li (2020) tested one of them. If STEM premiums have an effect and earnings metrics do not, pooling them under one binary attenuates the estimate toward zero by construction — and the paper's own state tables show that workforce-PBF status is coded on for many state-years where the STEM component is small or absent. The second difference is the outcome: Li examined both the number and the share of STEM bachelor's degrees, whereas this paper uses logged counts throughout. The share outcome is the direct test of compositional reallocation, which is exactly what the paper's own theoretical framing invokes when it hypothesizes that high-dosage PBF 'may work to encourage institutions to cluster students... toward or away from certain fields.' The framing sets up a compositional question and the outcome variable answers a volume question. Neither difference is disqualifying, but a reader who does not notice them will over-update against Li.

**Statistical positioning compounds this.** The paper reports a minimum detectable effect of roughly 9% for the 4-year sector and 11% for the 2-year sector at its Bonferroni-adjusted alphas (.0028 and .0015, i.e., 99.72% and 99.99% confidence intervals). It handles this responsibly in the abstract sense — it names the Type II risk, cites Feise (2002) and Gelman et al. (2012) as critics of Bonferroni, and reports relaxed-alpha results in the appendix — and it flags reduced power for small subfields like computer science. What it never does is bring that floor into contact with the literature comparison. 'Our results diverged from previous research on PBF policies with STEM premiums' is stated as a substantive disagreement about the world, when it may be a disagreement about evidentiary thresholds: an effect that Li (2020) detected at conventional significance would need to exceed roughly 9% to register here. Readers using this paper as evidence that field-based incentives fail should look at the confidence intervals in Figures 1 and 4 and ask what magnitudes they actually exclude, rather than reading 'not significant' as 'no effect.'

**On the novelty claim.** The paper makes it twice, in two different registers. On page 3 it says, correctly and carefully: 'We extend the literature by examining how the effects of workforce-oriented incentives vary by credential or institution type, extend to high-ROI fields beyond STEM, and vary by student race/ethnicity. We also contribute to the literature by exploring how workforce-oriented incentives affect non-incentivized or non-high-ROI fields.' Every clause there is defensible. Two pages later, closing the literature review, it says: 'To date, however, we do not have evidence of the extent to which field and ROI metrics in PBF models and policy dosage impact degree completion across different fields of study, especially among RM students and at non-4-year colleges.' Strip the 'especially' clause and this is false by the paper's own account of Li (2020) three pages earlier. The 'especially' clause is where the truth lives, and it is doing more work than its subordinate grammar suggests. This is a common and mostly forgivable pattern — the gap sentence is a genre convention — but it is the sentence most likely to be quoted, and it is the wrong one.

**On self-citation.** I would not call it excessive. Roughly a dozen of about eighty references are in-group, and the group genuinely produced the relevant corpus; excluding it would leave the paper unable to describe the policy landscape it is studying. Outside work is engaged substantively rather than perfunctorily — Hillman appears three times with accurate characterizations, Boland twice, Chan et al. once, Gándara & Rutherford once. The concern is narrower and more specific: the in-group citations supply the analytic conventions, not just the background. The 10% high-dosage threshold is justified by citing two prior in-group papers that used the same threshold, which is a convention rather than a validation. The PBF policy coding comes from the group's own dataset with no external cross-check. The finding is framed as consistent with a literature that is substantially the group's own. None of this is misconduct; it is what happens when one team owns both the measurement instrument and most of the estimates. Readers should hold the results with that structure in mind.

**On grey literature.** Cooper (2024) is the case that gives me most pause, because it is not decorative. It appears in the sentence defining the study's outcome taxonomy: 'High-ROI fields included STEM, business, and health majors, while the low-ROI fields included education, humanities, and arts majors (Andrews et al., 2024; Cooper, 2024; Zhang et al., 2024).' Two peer-reviewed sources flank it there, so the taxonomy is triangulated. But elsewhere Cooper stands alone for the claims that completion is the crucial first step for ROI and that sub-baccalaureate returns track field demand regardless of level. FREOPP is a policy-advocacy organization with a stated view about the value of higher education, and ROI estimates are notoriously sensitive to the counterfactual-earnings assumption, cost inputs, and discount rate. Bleemer et al. (2023) presents the same issue in smaller form: it is cited three times, including for a strong comparative claim about majors versus institutions in racial earnings stratification, and it is a Brookings commentary rather than the underlying peer-reviewed research. In both cases peer-reviewed alternatives exist and are known to these authors — some are already in the reference list.

**On accuracy of characterizations more broadly.** The PBF citations are, with one exception, handled well; this is a group that knows this literature and the Hillman and Li & Ortagus descriptions are faithful. The exception is Li (2017) on the theory page, cited for institutional programmatic response when the paper is about state adoption and policy diffusion — and notably, the same reference is used correctly later in the methods discussion, which suggests carelessness rather than misunderstanding. The framing-literature citations are looser than the PBF ones: the college-degree-versus-associate-degree sentence is internally incoherent in a paper about credential heterogeneity, the racial-IRR claim attributed to Zhang et al. (2024) is stronger than that paper's framing, and the Bleemer decomposition claim is a heavy load for a blog post. The reference list itself has a genuine error that will misdirect readers — Belfield & Bailey (2011) carries the Baker, Larcker & Wang (2022) JFE DOI, a copy-paste from the entry directly above it — plus a wrong article number for Pierszalowski et al. and two unclosed parentheses.

**On what the literature review does not reach.** Two absences seem consequential. First, the implementation and mechanisms literature. The paper's central interpretive claim is that PBF failed because dosage was too low and STEM premiums were a small share of a small share — a claim about how incentives propagate through institutions. That is precisely the terrain that Dougherty and colleagues mapped qualitatively across leading PBF states, and the paper draws on one 2014 working paper from that program, once, for a narrow point about costs. It then closes by calling for the qualitative work that partly exists. Second, the causal-resources literature. The paper's policy recommendation — fund institutions upfront rather than conditionally — is a causal claim about the returns to institutional spending, and it is made with no causal citation. Hemelt et al. (2021) establishes that STEM and health credentials cost more to produce, which is a necessary premise but not the conclusion. Deming & Walters and the Bound–Turner line of work supply the missing causal step.

**Bottom line for readers.** The literature review is competent, current, and unusually forthright about conflicting evidence — its willingness to name Li (2020) and the Hillman certificate findings and argue with them is a real virtue. Its weaknesses are concentrated and specific rather than diffuse: an asymmetric reconciliation with its one true competitor, a gap claim that overstates what was unknown, an undisclosed overlap with the authors' own closest working paper, a load-bearing think-tank source, and a handful of citation errors. Use the paper's PBF characterizations with confidence; verify its framing-literature claims before repeating them; and do not let its discussion section be the last word on Li (2020).

**Limits of my assessment.** I read the full text and reference list, and I verified the internal points — the DOI error, the Li (2017) mismatch, the citation counts, the inconsistency between the two novelty framings, the MDE figures — directly against the document. My knowledge of the PBF subfield is good but not exhaustive, so the omissions I list in the suggestions are flagged as leads to check rather than confirmed gaps; I am most confident about the thinness of the Dougherty-line implementation literature and the missing causal-resources citation, and least confident about the specific attribution details of the Ward & Ost, Bell et al., and Rutherford & Rabovsky studies. I did not independently re-read Li (2020), Zhang et al. (2024), or Cooper (2024), so my characterizations of what those sources actually claim rest on prior knowledge and should themselves be verified.

---

### Writing Review

**Rating:** Weak (high confidence)

Sentence-level prose is clean and the figure notes are unusually complete, but the paper's exposition does not faithfully carry its own evidence: a 545-word Results section containing zero coefficient estimates supports a 1,950-word Discussion that makes substantive-null claims, and the balance paragraph on pp. 7-8 misreports numbers a reader can check against Tables 4-7 in at least four places. The abstract's flat "did not have a significant impact" conceals that significance was judged at 99.72%/99.99% confidence with a 9-11% minimum detectable effect, that parallel trends fail for several outcomes, and that high-dosage estimates rest on very few post-periods. A reader who trusts the prose rather than re-deriving from the exhibits will come away with a materially stronger impression of the null than the evidence licenses.

**Strengths:**

- Figure notes (pp. 17-21) are exemplary and self-contained: each states the outcome and its log transform, the sample, all three treatment definitions, the comparison group, panel contents, covariates, fixed effects, clustering, and — critically — the multiple-comparison-adjusted alpha and the corresponding CI level (99.72% or 99.99%). This is more disclosure than most event-study papers provide, and it is the single most useful thing on the page.
- Y-axis scaling is held constant at -.8 to .8 across all 80 subplots in Figures 1-5, so panels are visually comparable across fields, credentials, and institution types. Panel A/B (all students vs. racially minoritized students) is a consistent, easily learned convention.
- The Limitations subsection (pp. 15-16) is candid and specific, naming the mechanism black box, the two-digit CIP mismatch with state formulas, non-uniform parallel trends, and the shortage of post-treatment periods for late high-dosage adopters. It is the most honest prose in the paper.
- The Method's power discussion (p. 15) is a genuine service: it reports MDEs of ~9% (4-year) and ~11% (2-year) at the preferred alpha and explicitly warns that smaller subfields are less well powered. Few null-results papers state this at all.
- Tables 1 and 2 are a real reference asset — state-by-state, year-by-year coding of any/workforce/high-dosage PBF for both sectors, with footnotes on system-level exclusions. These will outlive the paper's findings.
- The Discussion's dosage-arithmetic passage (pp. 20-22) is the paper's best explanatory writing: Michigan's STEM metric inside a <2% PBF system, of which STEM was ~20%; Pennsylvania's 4%; Texas's 2 of 12 points. It makes the null mechanically intelligible rather than merely asserted.

**Weaknesses:**

- The balance paragraph (pp. 7-8) — the paper's only evidence of comparability, since no formal balance test is reported — misstates its own tables repeatedly. "RM students accounted for similar shares of total completions... approximately 15% to 17% at 4-year institutions and 17% to 20% at 2-year institutions" does not match Tables 4-5: 4-year bachelor's RM shares are 17.8/15.6/15.6/20.8% and 2-year associate RM shares are 17.9/21.8/23.3/27.2%. The high-dosage 2-year column (27.2%) is 9 points above the never-PBF column (17.9%) and lies far outside the stated band.
- Same paragraph: "this difference was less than 50 degrees" — Table 4 gives 1,733.27 vs 1,680.80 = 52.47. And the high-dosage column (1,588.56) differs from never-PBF by 144.71 degrees, a gap the sentence does not acknowledge.
- Same paragraph: "While states that never adopted PBF tended to have larger total populations, treatment and comparison states had similar racial/ethnic population compositions." Both halves fail in the 2-year sector. Table 7: never-PBF White population 3,878,035 vs any-PBF 7,652,613 — the direction is reversed. Hispanic population 510,481 vs 3,281,595 (6.4x) and Asian 174,309 vs 979,129 (5.6x) — compositions are not similar. Never-PBF 2-year in-state tuition is 3,645 vs 1,702 in high-dosage states, more than double.
- Sample counts contradict each other. p. 7: "The sample includes 446 four-year and 807 two-year institutions" — then in the next paragraph the identical figure 446 is reused for a different quantity: "27 states (446 institutions) adopted PBF." Both cannot hold given a never-adopter comparison group. Table 4's Ns sum to 185+248 = 433 (not 446); Table 5's to 168+614 = 782 (not 807), and 614 contradicts the text's 626 for the 2-year sector.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** Partly withdrawn. Every table note says the descriptive statistics are for the base year (2003), and institutions in the 2003–2020 panel that are absent from the base year account for the gaps: 446 − 433 = 13 four-year institutions, and 807 − 782 = 25 two-year (12 of the 626 adopters and 13 of the 181 comparison institutions). The working paper's pre-exclusion 526/916 minus footnote 3's removals gives 447/807.
