So 446, 807 and 626 are consistent with the tables as panel totals, though the article never says so, and the MDE calculation, which uses the totals, is unaffected. What does not reconcile is p. 7's "27 states (446 institutions) adopted PBF": 446 is the whole four-year sample, and with 185 never-adopters in Table 4 the treated count must lie between 248 and 261. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered tables and the working paper.

- Results is 545 words and reports not a single coefficient, standard error, or confidence bound. There is no table of estimates. The five main figures contain roughly 2,500 point estimates, none recoverable numerically; the ~36 supplemental figures that carry the entire robustness argument are equally unreadable. A reader cannot quote an effect size or a CI width from this paper.
- Rhetoric outruns the evidence on substantive nulls. p. 19: "in statistically or substantively significant ways"; p. 23: "not moving the needle in substantive or statistically significant ways." The paper's own MDE is 9-11% for the aggregate outcomes at the preferred alpha and worse for subfields; Figure 3's high-dosage certificate intervals in engineering span roughly -0.85 to +0.95 in logs (about -57% to +160%). Those data cannot distinguish "no effect" from a large effect, and neither the Discussion nor the abstract carries the MDE or the CI level forward from the Method.
- The abstract's "did not have a significant impact" is unqualified. It omits the Bonferroni thresholds (alpha .0028/.0015, i.e. 99.72%/99.99% CIs), the MDE, the pre-trend violations the Results itself concedes, and the thin post-treatment window for high-dosage. "These results remained consistent across institution types" also overstates: the main text reports institution-type splits only for bachelor's degrees (Figures 4-5), the 2-year Carnegie splits live in Supplemental Figures A31-A34 (footnote 1), and Figure 4 flags high-dosage effects on doctoral health completions as deviating from zero.
- Broken cross-reference in Results (p. 16): a robustness claim cites "a more restrictive treatment group (Supplemental Appendix Figure A4)." But the Method (p. 8) assigns A1-A5 to no-control models and A16-A25 to sample restrictions. A reader following the pointer lands on the wrong figure.
- Equation 1 (p. 10) is misspecified as printed. The outcome is written y_{i,s} — indexed by institution and state, with no time index — while the surrounding text calls it y_{i,t+l}, introducing an undefined subscript l; neither matches the y_{it} the fixed effects (gamma_i, delta_t) and error (epsilon_it) require. The exclusion of the reference period is jammed into the summation's upper limit as "k=5, k=-1" rather than written as k != -1. And PBF_{i,t+k} is glossed as "1 if institution i adopted PBF k years before t," which inverts the sign convention the subscript implies.
- The Results sentence "For Education and Public Services, the coefficient estimates for 5 years and beyond are significantly different from zero" reads naturally as post-treatment, but Figure 2 Panel A shows the violation at k = -5 (about -0.35, interval excluding zero) with a monotone convergence to zero by k = -1 — a textbook pre-trend that can mechanically manufacture a null. The reader must open the figure to parse the sentence correctly, and the Discussion never mentions it.
- The theoretical framework's one testable institution-level prediction — "We hypothesize that doctoral universities will be more likely to meet PBF goals because they have more available resources" (p. 6) — is never revisited. Figures 4 and 5 exist to test it, but the words "doctoral" and "baccalaureate" do not appear anywhere in the Discussion.
- Table 7 contains an uncorrected numeric typo: never-PBF State Black population is printed as "8,379,70.43" for 837,970.43. At a glance it reads as 8.4 million, an order of magnitude off, in the very row a reader would use to judge comparison-group composition.
- Table 5's certificate rows do not reconcile: short-term (256.28) + long-term (135.43) = 391.71 against a stated Total of 277.30 for never-PBF states; 205.19 + 104.56 = 309.75 against 259.29 for any-PBF. The note offers no denominator that would explain the gap.
- Table 1 is titled "Funded PBF Policies for the 4-Year Sector, 2003 to 2020" but the South Carolina row reads 1998-2002 — entirely outside the window — so a reader counting treated states from the table gets 26 in-window, not the 27 the text claims. Relatedly, footnote 3's exclusion lists differ by sector (Florida dropped from 2-year but present in Table 1; Ohio dropped from 4-year but present in Table 2) with no explanation, and Pennsylvania — excluded from the 4-year sample by footnote 3 — is used in the Discussion (p. 21) as an illustrative 4-year STEM-incentive case.
- Certificate interpretation in the Discussion (p. 22) converts a null into a mechanism: "PBF policies that focus on student ROI may have reduced or eliminated institutions' incentives for promoting certificate completion." Nothing in Figure 3 tests this, and the Results had just warned that parallel-trends support is "weaker" for long-term certificates.
- "It is encouraging that the PBF policies analyzed here do not seem to negatively impact RM students' completion" (p. 22) reads absence of evidence as evidence of absence, on a subgroup with roughly one-sixth the completion counts (Table 4: 308 vs 1,733 bachelor's) and therefore wider intervals, judged at 99.72%/99.99% confidence.
- Structural placement works against the reader: Limitations sits inside the Method, before Results, so its caveats are delivered before the reader has seen the exhibits they qualify and are never restated afterward; the Discussion (1,950 words) is 3.6x the Results it interprets; there is no Conclusion or Implications heading, and the paper's main policy suggestion ("providing more financial resources to institutions upfront") is buried mid-Discussion on p. 23.
- Table 6 is titled "Descriptive Statistics for State Characteristics: 4-year Institutions" but roughly half its rows (in-state tuition, grant aid, aid recipients, FTE enrollment, instructional expenditure) are institution-level. Its 2-year twin, Table 7, is titled "Descriptive Statistics for Covariates" — two titles for identical content.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Do not quote the abstract's finding without the Method's qualifiers. Read p. 15 (Bonferroni alpha .0028/.0015; MDE ~9% for 4-year, ~11% for 2-year) and the figure notes on pp. 17-21 (99.72%/99.99% CIs) before repeating "did not have a significant impact." The correct paraphrase is: at extremely conservative multiple-comparison-adjusted thresholds, no effect larger than roughly 9-11% was detected for the aggregate outcomes, with less power for subfields.
- Treat the balance paragraph on pp. 7-8 as unreliable and re-derive it. Every quantitative claim in it that I checked was off: the RM completion shares (actual 15.6-20.8% at 4-year, 17.9-27.2% at 2-year), the "less than 50 degrees" gap (52.47, and 144.71 against high-dosage), and the population-size direction (reversed in Table 7). Compute the ratios yourself from Tables 4-7 before relying on any statement about comparability, especially for the 2-year sector, where the never-PBF states look sharply different on tuition and demographic composition.
- For the actual findings, skip the Results text and go to the figures. Focus on Figure 3 (certificates) and the high-dosage series in every panel: look at the width of the open-circle intervals, several of which run past the last labeled tick at ±.8, and note that the 99.99% adjustment makes visual non-significance nearly automatic. Figure 2 Panel A, Education & Public Service, is the panel to inspect closely — the k = -5 pre-trend the text describes obliquely as "5 years and beyond."
- Do not read the Discussion's "substantively" null claims (pp. 19 and 23) as established. Hold them against the Method's MDE paragraph on p. 15 and the Limitations on pp. 15-16, both of which say the opposite — that effects of policy-relevant size, especially in subfields and for recently adopted high-dosage policies, would not be detectable here.
- Read the Limitations (pp. 15-16) before the Results, not after — it is physically placed there and it is the most accurate account of what the design can and cannot show. Nothing in the Discussion restates it.
- If you need sample sizes, use the N rows in Tables 4 and 5 (185/248 for 4-year, 168/614 for 2-year), not the text. The text's "446" is used for two incompatible quantities on p. 7, and its "626" for the 2-year treated group contradicts Table 5's 614.
- Cite Tables 1 and 2 as the paper's most durable output — the state-by-year PBF design coding for both sectors. Two cautions when reusing them: South Carolina's 4-year row (1998-2002) falls outside the stated 2003-2020 window, and footnote 3 (pp. 23-24) removes several states from the estimation samples asymmetrically by sector, so the tables are not the analytic sample.
- Check any number you plan to reproduce from Table 7 — the never-PBF Black population is printed as "8,379,70.43" and should read 837,970.43. Likewise, do not add Table 5's short-term and long-term certificate rows: they exceed the stated certificate total in every column, and no note explains why.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** Not every column. The short- plus long-term certificate rows exceed the certificate total only in the four all-student columns, by 50 to 114; the subgroup columns add up. The same pattern appears in the working paper, so it sits in the variable construction; which cell is wrong cannot be settled from the public record. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered table.

- Skim the Literature Review and Theoretical Framework (pp. 3-7) — they are competent and conventional, and the barriers-to-STEM material is background rather than load-bearing. The one item worth marking is the doctoral-vs-master's hypothesis on p. 6, because Figures 4-5 test it and the Discussion never returns to it; if you care about institutional heterogeneity, you must read those figures unaided by the prose.
- Read Equation 1 on p. 10 as a typeset artifact rather than a specification. The outcome subscripts are inconsistent across the equation and the paragraph beneath it, and the reference-period exclusion is written into the summation limit. The intended model is a standard Sun-Abraham event study with institution and year fixed effects and state-clustered errors — take that from the surrounding text, not the display.
- The Discussion's most substantive contribution is the dosage arithmetic on pp. 20-22 (Michigan, Pennsylvania, Texas). Read it — it is the paper's real explanation for the null. But note that Pennsylvania's 4-year institutions were excluded from the sample by footnote 3, so the example illustrates rather than evidences.
- Discount the Discussion's causal reading of the certificate null on p. 22 ("PBF policies that focus on student ROI may have reduced or eliminated institutions' incentives") and the reassurance on the RM subgroup ("it is encouraging that... do not seem to negatively impact"). Neither is tested; both convert a wide, conservatively thresholded null into a directional conclusion.

**Detailed Commentary:**

ORGANIZATION AND NAVIGABILITY. The paper follows the EEPA convention (unheaded introduction, Literature Review p. 3, Theoretical Framework p. 5, Data and Method p. 6, Analytic Approach p. 9, Limitations p. 15, Results p. 16, Discussion p. 17) with one consequential departure: Limitations is a subsection of the Method and appears before Results. The practical effect is that the paper's most accurate self-assessment — non-uniform parallel trends, few post-periods for high-dosage adopters, two-digit CIP codes that may not match state formulas — is delivered before the reader has seen a single exhibit and is never repeated once the exhibits have been shown. The Discussion, at roughly 1,950 words against a 545-word Results, therefore reads as if those caveats had been discharged. There is no Conclusion or Implications heading; the paper stops mid-Discussion after the "not moving the needle" paragraph, and the one forward-looking policy suggestion (upfront funding rather than performance conditioning) is stranded on p. 23 rather than positioned where a policy reader would find it.

The load-bearing material is in three places, none of them the Results text. First, Tables 1 and 2 (pp. 8, 9), the state-by-year policy coding that is the paper's most reusable contribution. Second, Figures 1-5 (pp. 17-21), which contain the entire evidentiary basis. Third, the Method's power paragraph (p. 15), which is the only place a reader learns what "not significant" means here. Everything else — the Literature Review's ~1,200 words on major-specific returns and STEM barriers, the Theoretical Framework's principal-agent exposition — is skimmable background.

RESULTS SECTION. Five hundred forty-five words, no numbers. The only numerals in the section are figure references and the alternate alpha of 0.01. There is no table of estimates and no summary count of how many coefficients were significant. Figures 1-5 contain approximately 2,500 point estimates (Figure 1 alone: 8 fields x 2 panels x 3 treatments x 11 event times = 528), and the robustness argument rests on roughly 36 supplemental figures of comparable density. A reader cannot extract a single effect size or interval bound from the article. Prose stands in for estimates throughout: "generally not significantly distinguishable from zero," "showed some variation in point estimates," "without consistent patterns of statistical significance." The one place the text does quantify uncertainty — "Coefficient estimates on the effects of high-dosage PBF policies tend to have wide confidence intervals" — is exactly where a number would matter most and none is given.

FIGURES. Y-axis scaling is admirably consistent (-.8 to .8, .2 increments, across all 80 subplots). Against that, three problems. Panels are roughly 1.5 inches wide and carry three overlaid series (filled triangle = any PBF, x = workforce, open circle = high-dosage) jittered by about a third of an event-period; at print size the x marker is frequently obscured by the triangle, so the workforce series — one of the paper's two headline policy designs — is the hardest of the three to read. Second, intervals routinely extend past the last labeled tick: in Figure 3 Panel A, Engineering, the high-dosage whiskers at k = 2, 3, 4 run to roughly ±0.95, so the reader must extrapolate beyond the axis labels to see how uninformative those estimates are. The exhibit thereby visually understates the uncertainty the text acknowledges in passing. Third, no axis carries a units label; that the coefficients are log points is disclosed only in the notes ("Number of bachelor's degrees awarded (logged)"). The notes are otherwise the best-executed element of the paper — sample, treatments, comparison group, covariates, fixed effects, clustering, and the adjusted alpha with its CI percentage are all stated — though they omit per-arm Ns and never say whether k = -5 and k = +5 are binned endpoints, which the Results' phrase "5 years and beyond" hints at without confirming.

TEXT-TABLE FIDELITY. This is where the paper fails most clearly, and it fails in the paragraph that does the most work. Pages 7-8 carry the only balance evidence in the article (no formal balance test is reported), and I could not confirm any of its quantitative claims. (a) "approximately 15% to 17% at 4-year institutions and 17% to 20% at 2-year institutions" — Table 4 gives 17.8/15.6/15.6/20.8%; Table 5 associate gives 17.9/21.8/23.3/27.2% and certificates 25.8-29.1%. The high-dosage 2-year figure exceeds the stated ceiling by seven points. (b) "this difference was less than 50 degrees" — Table 4 yields 52.47 for never-PBF vs any-PBF, and 144.71 vs high-dosage. (c) "states that never adopted PBF tended to have larger total populations" and "similar racial/ethnic population compositions" — true in Table 6 (4-year), reversed and false in Table 7 (2-year), where never-PBF states have half the White population, one-sixth the Hispanic population, and more than double the in-state tuition of high-dosage states. Because the balance paragraph explicitly spans both sectors ("At both 4-year and 2-year institutions..."), a reader has no cue that its conclusions hold for only one.

Sample counts compound this. Page 7 states a total sample of 446 four-year and 807 two-year institutions, then reuses 446 one paragraph later for the number of institutions in PBF-adopting states — mutually exclusive given a never-adopter comparison group. Table 4's Ns sum to 433 and Table 5's to 782, neither matching the stated totals, and Table 5's treated N of 614 contradicts the text's 626. The MDE calculation on p. 15 uses 446 and 807, so the discrepancy propagates into the power claim.

Smaller traps: Table 7 prints "8,379,70.43" for 837,970.43; Table 5's short-term plus long-term certificates exceed the certificate total in every column (391.71 vs 277.30; 309.75 vs 259.29) with no denominator note; Table 1's title says 2003-2020 while South Carolina's row reads 1998-2002; footnote 3 drops Florida from the 2-year sample though Florida appears in Table 1, and drops Ohio from the 4-year sample though Ohio appears in Table 2, without a word of explanation; the Method promises that "the full list of academic fields included in the study for each credential type is reported in Table 3," but Table 3 has only Field and CIP columns and no credential-type breakdown; Table 6 and Table 7 carry different titles ("State Characteristics" vs "Covariates") for identical content, and Table 6's title is wrong given that half its rows are institution-level. Finally, the Results' robustness pointer to "a more restrictive treatment group (Supplemental Appendix Figure A4)" contradicts the Method's own mapping, in which A1-A5 are the no-control models and A16-A25 are the sample restrictions.

> **Correction (2026-09-26).** Not every column. The short- plus long-term certificate rows exceed the certificate total only in the four all-student columns, by 50 to 114; the subgroup columns add up. The same pattern appears in the working paper, so it sits in the variable construction; which cell is wrong cannot be settled from the public record. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered table.

EQUATION 1 (p. 10). Verified against the rendered PDF, so these are not extraction artifacts. The outcome is typeset as y_{i,s} — institution and state, no time index — while the paragraph beneath refers to y_{i,t+l} with an l that is never defined; neither is the y_{it} implied by gamma_i, delta_t, and epsilon_it. The summation is printed with limits "k=-5" to "k=5, k=-1," folding the reference-period exclusion into the upper limit instead of writing k != -1. And PBF_{i,t+k} is glossed as equaling 1 "if institution i adopted PBF k years before t," which inverts the timing the subscript states. A reader tracing the sign and timing conventions will have to reconstruct the specification from the Sun-Abraham citation rather than the display.

FIDELITY OF ARGUMENT. Three claims outrun the evidence. First, substantive nulls: "in statistically or substantively significant ways" (p. 19) and "not moving the needle in substantive or statistically significant ways" (p. 23). The paper's own MDE is 9-11% for aggregate outcomes at the preferred alpha, explicitly worse for subfields, and Figure 3's high-dosage certificate intervals span roughly -57% to +160% in levels. The design can rule out nothing substantive; the Method says so and the Discussion says the reverse. The 99.72%/99.99% CI levels never appear outside the figure notes, and the MDE never appears outside p. 15 — so a reader moving from Method to Discussion loses both qualifiers exactly where they are needed.

Second, the certificate mechanism (p. 22): "PBF policies that focus on student ROI may have reduced or eliminated institutions' incentives for promoting certificate completion." This reads a null as evidence that a previously documented incentive was removed. No test of that proposition is reported, and the Results had just flagged long-term certificates as an outcome where parallel-trends support is weaker.

Third, the equity reassurance (p. 22): "it is encouraging that the PBF policies analyzed here do not seem to negatively impact RM students' completion." The RM subgroup has roughly one-sixth the completion counts of the full sample (Table 4: 308.04 vs 1,733.27 bachelor's), hence wider intervals, evaluated at 99.72-99.99% confidence. The sentence converts a low-powered null into good news, then partially retracts itself two sentences later ("future research should investigate this in more detail").

CAUSAL LANGUAGE. The paper never settles. The title says "Examining the Impact"; all three research questions ask "to what extent do PBF policies... impact"; the Analytic Approach opens "To estimate the impact of PBF." But the purpose statement one paragraph before the RQs says "are associated with," the Results conclusion says "does not appear to be associated with statistically significant changes," and the Discussion says "we did not find evidence of PBF policies being associated with improved completion outcomes." The abstract lands on the strong end ("did not have a significant impact"), which is the version most readers will carry away, and it is the version least supported by a design the Limitations concede has pre-trend violations for some outcomes.

UNRETURNED THREAD. The Theoretical Framework's only testable institution-level prediction — "We hypothesize that doctoral universities will be more likely to meet PBF goals because they have more available resources to support students and departments" (p. 6) — is what Figures 4 and 5 exist to test. The Results reports both groups as null in four sentences and does not mention the hypothesis. The words "doctoral" and "baccalaureate" appear nowhere in the Discussion. A reader who came for the institutional-heterogeneity argument gets the setup and the exhibits but no interpretation connecting them.

ABSTRACT. Two sentences of findings, both unqualified. "PBF policies did not have a significant impact on completion for certificates, associate degrees, or bachelor's degrees across fields of study" omits the multiple-comparison thresholds, the MDE, and the parallel-trends failures. "These results remained consistent across institution types and students' racial/ethnic background" overstates on both counts: institution-type analyses in the main text cover bachelor's degrees only, the 2-year Carnegie splits are relegated to Supplemental Figures A31-A34 via footnote 1, and Figure 4 itself shows high-dosage effects on health completions at doctoral universities deviating from zero in some post-treatment periods — a caveat "consistent" erases. For a paper whose contribution is a null, the abstract needed to convey how conservative the inference was; it conveys the opposite.

WHAT A TIME-CONSTRAINED READER SHOULD DO. Read Tables 1-2 for the policy coding, p. 15 for what the design can detect, pp. 15-16 for the limitations, and Figures 2 and 3 for the estimates that matter (the pre-trend in associate Education & Public Service, and the high-dosage certificate intervals). Skim the Literature Review and Theoretical Framework. Read the Discussion's dosage arithmetic on pp. 20-22, which is genuinely illuminating, and discount its concluding rhetoric. Re-derive anything from the balance paragraph before citing it.

---

### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

This paper delivers the first national, event-study evidence on two newer performance-based funding (PBF) design features — workforce/ROI-oriented completion metrics and high-dosage (≥10%) funding formulas — estimated on completions disaggregated by credential type (bachelor's, associate, short/long certificate) and CIP-2 field, overall and for racially minoritized (RM) students, using the InformEd States policy database for 2003–2020 and modern staggered-adoption estimators (Sun–Abraham, Gardner). Its contribution is a well-executed, broadly scoped null: it extends the existing PBF null-results literature to a margin (field-of-study composition of completions) where prior work had found the field's two most cited positive/behavioral results, and it fails to reproduce either. The contribution is real and useful but incremental and narrower than the abstract implies — the workforce treatment is a bundled construct, the paper reports no numeric coefficients or confidence intervals anywhere, and the precision needed to license the strong 'no effect' reading exists only for aggregate outcomes, not for the field × credential × race cells that are the paper's actual novelty.

**Strengths:**

- Genuinely new margin of analysis. Prior PBF work has estimated effects on total degrees, graduation rates, enrollment, and appropriations. This is the first study to take field-of-study composition as the outcome across all three credential levels simultaneously, at national scale, for both the 2-year and 4-year sectors. The question is well-motivated: if PBF works at all, design theory (principal–agent, selective attention, gaming) predicts it should show up as reallocation across programs rather than as a level shift in total output — which is exactly what earlier aggregate nulls could not detect.
- Targets the two design features that actually characterize contemporary PBF. Most of the PBF evidence base evaluates the 2000s-era 'any PBF' binary, which policymakers have long since moved past. Studying workforce/ROI premiums and the ≥10% dosage threshold puts the evidence closer to the policies states are currently writing, and the InformEd States data (Ortagus et al., 2021) is the best available source for coding those features longitudinally.
- Unusually thorough sensitivity architecture for a null. The design is stress-tested against a real menu of alternatives: three estimators (Sun–Abraham, Gardner two-stage, conventional TWFE), a never-treated comparison group and a design-specific comparison group (PBF adopters without the workforce premium / without high dosage), a treatment group restricted to non-abandoners, models with and without covariates, an alternative Carnegie split for 2-year colleges, exclusion of mixed baccalaureate/associate colleges, and both Bonferroni-adjusted and relaxed (α ≤ .01) significance criteria. Roughly 36 appendix figures back this up. A null supported by this many crossings is more credible than most nulls in this literature.
- The paper explicitly computes minimum detectable effects (~9% for 4-year, ~11% for 2-year) rather than treating statistical insignificance as evidence of absence by default, and it names the right caveat — that smaller subfields with high variance in degree production support weaker inferences.
- The limitations section is honest about the three things that most constrain the result: no visibility into institutional mechanisms, CIP-2 coding that cannot match state formulas that may incentivize narrow programs, and few post-treatment periods for the recent high-dosage and workforce adopters. Readers are told where parallel trends fail (associate-level education/public service; computer science and long-term certificates) rather than having to infer it.

**Weaknesses:**

- The paper reports no numeric estimates anywhere. Tables 1–7 are policy timelines and baseline descriptives; every result lives in five figures of event-study plots (plus ~36 appendix figures), with no coefficient table, no standard errors, and no interval endpoints in the text. A reader cannot extract a point estimate or an upper bound for any outcome, cannot enter this study into a meta-analysis, and cannot check whether a given field's 'null' rules out a 5% effect or a 40% one. For a paper whose entire contribution is the precision of a null, this is the single largest limitation on its usability.
- The stated MDEs do not apply to the paper's novel outcomes. The ~9%/11% figures are computed for total bachelor's degrees and total associate/certificate awards. The field × credential × race cells — the study's actual innovation — are far smaller and noisier. Baseline descriptives make this concrete: RM associate degrees in engineering average 2.5–3.1 per institution, RM certificates in engineering 1.6–3.8, RM bachelor's in agriculture/natural resources 2.6–3.8. Logged counts of two or three awards per institution-year cannot support a meaningful null, and the figures show correspondingly wide intervals (many spanning roughly ±0.2 to ±0.4 log points, wider for high-dosage). The Bonferroni adjustment (99.72%/99.99% CIs) widens them further. The abstract's flat claim of 'no significant impact ... across fields of study' is therefore substantially stronger than the estimates it rests on.
- The 'workforce PBF' treatment bundles two conceptually distinct incentives. It codes as identical (a) a premium for completions in designated high-demand/high-ROI fields, such as Nevada's STEM premium, and (b) metrics rewarding graduates' employment or earnings, which carry no field-specific instruction at all. Since the outcome is completions by field, only (a) generates the predicted signal; states with earnings/employment metrics alone dilute the treatment toward zero. With 226 of 446 four-year institutions coded as workforce-treated, this could be a large share of the treatment group. The paper acknowledges CIP-2 coarseness as a limitation but never flags the treatment-side bundling.
- The framing promises a test of student 'clustering' toward or away from fields, but the outcomes are logged counts of completions, never field shares or completions conditional on enrollment. Reallocation across majors — the composition change the theoretical framework predicts, and the outcome on which Li (2020) found STEM effects — is not directly estimated. A null on counts is consistent with meaningful compositional shifts if total completions moved in the same direction across fields.
- The divergences from Li (2020) and Hillman et al. (2015, 2018) are asserted, not adjudicated. Three explanations are offered (newer estimators, newer data, sample restrictions) but none is tested, even though the paper already has the ingredients: it reports conventional TWFE in the appendix and could show whether the estimator or the data drives the difference. Crucially, a mechanical explanation goes unmentioned — the pre-period-adopter exclusion (footnote 3) removes Tennessee from both sectors and Ohio from the 4-year sample, i.e., precisely the two states Hillman, Hicklin Fryar & Crespín-Trujillo (2018) studied. Failing to reproduce a certificate-shifting result in a sample that excludes the states where it was found is much weaker evidence against it than the Discussion implies.
- The Discussion's most quotable lines outrun the evidence. 'PBF policies that focus on student ROI may have reduced or eliminated institutions' incentives for promoting certificate completion' is a mechanism the design cannot identify (no ROI-metric-specific certificate contrast is estimated) and is confounded with the sample and estimator differences just described. 'Rather than conditioning state funding on performance metrics, providing more financial resources to institutions upfront may be a more effective way to improve completion' has no support in this paper at all — base appropriations are a covariate, never a treatment, and no comparison of funding modalities is attempted.
- The RM findings sit in unresolved tension with the same team's own prior work. Ortagus, Rosinger, Kelchen, Voorhees, Chu & Allchin (2023) — same policy database, overlapping period, overlapping authors — report that high-dosage PBF reduced bachelor's completion among RM students while increasing it among White students. Here, the disaggregated RM analyses show nothing, and the paper reads this as 'encouraging.' The more likely reading is that field-level RM cells are too noisy to recover an effect the aggregate analysis detected. The paper gives this one sentence and defers to future research rather than reconciling it.
- The analytic window largely predates the regimes the Discussion invokes. The paper closes by pointing to Texas allocating roughly 95% of community college funding by performance — a policy far outside the 2003–2020 data, and outside the 10% threshold this study can speak to. Many high-dosage adopters enter only in 2017–2020, leaving very few post-periods. The evidence is about a moderate-dosage world; the policy conversation it enters is about a high-dosage one.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- CITE IT FOR: the best current national evidence that PBF as implemented through 2020 — including systems with workforce/ROI premiums — did not produce large increases in completions in incentivized high-ROI fields (STEM, health, business) at public 4-year institutions. This is the paper's best-supported claim and its clearest advance over aggregate-only prior work.
- CITE IT FOR: a well-documented, transparently coded account of which states funded PBF, workforce premiums, and high-dosage formulas in which years, 2003–2020 (Tables 1 and 2). These tables are independently useful for anyone coding PBF policy.
- CITE IT FOR: the demonstration that the field-of-study reallocation channel — the leading explanation for why aggregate PBF nulls might mask real institutional responses — does not obviously rescue PBF's effectiveness case. This narrows the space of viable 'PBF works, we're just measuring it wrong' arguments.
- CITE IT FOR (with care): non-replication of Li (2020)'s STEM-premium result under staggered-adoption-robust estimators. Frame it as a failure to replicate under a different design, sample, and period — not as a refutation.
- DO NOT CITE IT FOR: 'PBF does not affect completion for RM students' or 'PBF is not harmful to RM students.' The RM × field × credential cells involve baseline counts of only a few awards per institution-year and produce intervals too wide to distinguish null from substantial harm; this null is uninformative and does not overturn the aggregate RM harm found by the same team in Ortagus et al. (2023).
- DO NOT CITE IT FOR: any specific effect size or upper bound on PBF effects. The paper reports no coefficients or interval endpoints, so no quantitative bound can be recovered from it, and the headline ~9%/11% MDEs apply to aggregate outcomes only, not to the field-level results.
- DO NOT CITE IT FOR: 'ROI-focused PBF eliminated the certificate-shifting behavior found by Hillman et al.' The design cannot identify that mechanism, and the 2-year sample excludes Tennessee (and the 4-year sample excludes Ohio and Tennessee) — the states where certificate shifting was originally documented.
- DO NOT CITE IT FOR: 'upfront funding beats performance funding.' That Discussion sentence is a policy conjecture; the paper never estimates any effect of base appropriations and offers no comparison of funding modalities.
- DO NOT CITE IT FOR: high-dosage PBF specifically. High-dosage adoption is concentrated in 2017–2020, leaving few post-periods and visibly the widest intervals in every figure; the paper's own limitations section says so. It is silent on the very-high-dosage regimes (e.g., Texas HB 8) now being adopted.
- STILL OPEN: whether program-level (rather than CIP-2) incentive coding would reveal effects that broad field aggregation masks — the authors name this as the key data gap and it is the most important follow-on.
- STILL OPEN: whether workforce PBF affects the composition (share) of completions across fields, as opposed to counts. Shares are the natural test of the steering/clustering mechanism the paper theorizes and never estimates.
- STILL OPEN: whether the divergence from Li (2020) is driven by the estimator, the policy coding, or the sample window — the paper lists three candidates and tests none, so the field should treat the Li result as contested rather than superseded.
- STILL OPEN: whether much-higher-dosage regimes (≥50% of funding) behave differently. This study's evidence stops at a 10% threshold and largely predates the current wave.
- STILL OPEN: the mechanism question. All of this literature, including this paper, infers institutional behavior from completion counts; nothing here observes advising, aid allocation, program closures, or curricular change, so offsetting responses remain untestable.

**Detailed Commentary:**

WHAT IS ACTUALLY NEW. Three things, in descending order of importance. First, the outcome margin: prior PBF evaluations estimate effects on totals (degrees, graduation rates, enrollment, appropriations); this paper estimates them on completions decomposed by CIP-2 field within each of four credential types (bachelor's, associate, short-term certificate, long-term certificate). That decomposition is the paper's real innovation, and it directly tests the most common defense of the aggregate null — that PBF reshuffles output across programs without changing its level. Second, the treatment margin: workforce/ROI-oriented premiums and the ≥10% dosage threshold are the design features that distinguish contemporary PBF from the systems most of the evidence base evaluates. Third, the estimator: Sun–Abraham as the main specification, with Gardner two-stage and TWFE as checks, applied to a staggered-adoption setting where earlier PBF studies used designs now known to be biased under treatment-effect heterogeneity.

What is not new is the bottom line. 'PBF does not increase completion' is the established finding (Ortagus et al., 2020; Hillman et al., 2014, 2015, 2018; Boland, 2020; Li & Ortagus, 2019), and the paper says so itself: 'Given previous null findings on the effects of PBF broadly for student success, it follows that our more granular approach to understanding completion outcomes yielded similar results.' The value added is that the null now survives disaggregation and survives extension to newer policy designs — a real but incremental consolidation, not a reversal.

WHAT THE NULL ACTUALLY RULES OUT. This is where readers most need to be careful, and where the abstract and the estimates diverge. The paper does the right thing by computing MDEs, but the reported ~9% (4-year) and ~11% (2-year) figures are derived for aggregate degree counts across 446 and 807 institutions over 18 years. They do not govern the field-level cells. Reading the figures, intervals in the field panels are visibly wide — many spanning roughly ±0.2 to ±0.4 log points, with high-dosage estimates wider still (the paper attributes this to the small number of high-dosage states). Bonferroni adjustment to 99.72%/99.99% coverage widens them further; the authors flag that this trades Type I for Type II error and report relaxed-alpha results in the appendix, but the main-text conclusion rests on the conservative version.

So the defensible statement is 'no evidence that PBF, workforce premiums, or high-dosage PBF produced large increases in completions in incentivized fields within roughly five post-adoption years.' The statement the abstract makes — 'PBF policies did not have a significant impact on completion for certificates, associate degrees, or bachelor's degrees across fields of study' — invites a stronger reading, and 'not moving the needle in substantive or statistically significant ways' invites it further. Because no coefficients or intervals appear anywhere in the paper, a reader cannot independently calibrate how strong a claim the data support. That is the central usability problem: a paper whose contribution is the informativeness of a null publishes no quantity from which informativeness can be judged.

The RM results are the sharpest instance. Baseline descriptives make the power problem concrete: RM associate degrees in engineering average 2.46–3.14 per institution; RM certificates in engineering 1.56–3.84; RM bachelor's degrees in agriculture/natural resources 2.55–3.83. Logged outcomes at those magnitudes, split by state-level treatment, clustered at the state level, and Bonferroni-adjusted, cannot distinguish a null from a large effect. The Discussion's 'it is encouraging that the PBF policies analyzed here do not seem to negatively impact RM students' completion' is the least-supported sentence in the paper — and it directly abuts the same team's finding (Ortagus, Rosinger, Kelchen, Voorhees, Chu & Allchin, 2023) that high-dosage PBF lowered RM bachelor's completion and raised White completion in overlapping data. The natural reading is not that PBF became safer, but that field-level disaggregation destroyed the power to see an effect the aggregate analysis found. The paper gestures at this ('future research should investigate this in more detail') but the equity-null will nonetheless get cited as reassurance.

CONSTRUCT VALIDITY OF THE TREATMENT. The workforce-PBF indicator covers both field-completion premiums and graduate employment/earnings metrics. Only the former carries a field-specific instruction, so a state with an earnings metric and no field premium contributes attenuation to an outcome defined by field. The paper's own examples show how thin the incentive can be even in the field-premium case — Michigan's STEM metric sat inside a system allocating under 2% of state funds, with STEM worth about 20% of PBF dollars; Pennsylvania's STEM bonus inside a 4% system; Texas's 10% system awarded 2 of 12 points for STEM. The authors use these to explain the null, which is a fair and important interpretive move. But it also means the study's real finding may be 'incentives this small do not move field-level output,' which is a narrower and more mechanical claim than 'workforce-oriented PBF design does not work.' The acknowledged CIP-2 coarseness compounds this from the outcome side: state formulas may target narrow programs inside broad fields. Both problems push toward attenuation, and neither is quantified.

RECONCILIATION WITH PRIOR WORK. The paper's most consequential moves for the field are its two non-replications, and both are handled thinly. Against Li (2020) on STEM premiums, three explanations are offered — newer DiD estimators, newer policy data, sample restrictions — and none is tested, despite the appendix already containing conventional TWFE estimates that could isolate the estimator channel. Against Hillman et al. on certificate substitution, the Discussion floats a substantive story (ROI-focused PBF removed the incentive to push certificates). But the exclusion of pre-period adopters removes Tennessee from both sectors and Ohio from the 4-year sample — Ohio and Tennessee being exactly the setting of Hillman, Hicklin Fryar & Crespín-Trujillo (2018). Non-replication in a sample that excludes the original states is weak evidence about the original finding, and the paper does not mention the overlap. Readers should treat both prior results as contested, not overturned.

WHAT THE FRAMING PROMISES BUT DOES NOT DELIVER. The theoretical framework is about steering: institutions clustering students, particularly minoritized students, toward or away from fields based on perceived likelihood of success. The natural test is field shares or completions conditional on enrollment. The paper estimates logged counts only. Li (2020) examined both number and share of STEM bachelor's degrees; not carrying the share outcome forward means the compositional hypothesis that motivates the study is never directly evaluated. A reader looking for evidence on major-steering will not find it here, only evidence on levels.

GENERALIZABILITY AND SHELF LIFE. The boundaries are drawn honestly in the limitations section, and the caveats are the right ones. But the paper's temporal reach is short in a way that matters for how it will be used. Most workforce-premium adoption is mid-to-late 2010s and most high-dosage adoption is 2017–2020, so the post-treatment windows for the study's novel treatments are thin, and effects requiring sustained institutional investment or departmental culture change — which the Discussion itself identifies as the likely mechanism — would not appear. The Discussion then invokes Texas's move to allocate roughly 95% of community college funding by performance with high-demand-field premiums. That is far outside anything estimated here. Cited carelessly, this paper will be used to argue that high-dosage workforce PBF does not work; what it shows is that PBF at dosages up to and modestly beyond 10%, observed for a handful of years, did not visibly change field-level completions.

STANDING. On its exact question — national effects of workforce-oriented and high-dosage PBF on completions by broad field and credential, 2003–2020 — this is now the best available evidence, because no comparable study exists. It should become the default citation for the proposition that field-targeted PBF incentives at typical dosages have not delivered, and its policy tables are a useful public good. It is not, however, the definitive test of whether field-targeted incentives can work: the treatment is bundled, the outcome is coarser than the policies, the compositional outcome is unexamined, and the precision is adequate only where the paper is least novel. It sets up a clear and well-specified research agenda — program-level incentive coding, share-based outcomes, longer post-periods, and direct evidence on institutional mechanisms — and the authors name most of it themselves. A solid, careful, honestly caveated contribution whose abstract and Discussion are more quotable than its estimates warrant.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Weak (high confidence)

All three data sources (IPEDS, Census, InformEd States PBF) are public or quasi-public, and the state-by-year policy coding is printed in full in Tables 1 and 2 — a genuine transparency asset that most PBF papers do not provide. But the article carries no data availability statement, no replication package, no posted code, and — most consequentially — not a single point estimate, standard error, confidence interval, or per-regression sample size anywhere in the text. The paper's entire evidentiary base is 5 densely gridded event-study figures plus 36 uncited-in-detail supplemental figures, so a reader cannot check the magnitude or the precision of any of the null results the paper is built on.

**Strengths:**

- Data sources are named and are among the most accessible in the field: IPEDS Completions and institutional finance/characteristics, Census state population and economic series, and the InformEd States PBF policy dataset (Ortagus, Rosinger, & Kelchen, 2021). None require a restricted-use application or a DUA, so the raw ingredients are in principle obtainable by any reader.
- Tables 1 and 2 print the complete treatment coding — every state, every funded PBF year, and separately the workforce-premium years and high-dosage years, for the 4-year and 2-year sectors respectively. This is the single most valuable transparency element in the paper: it lets a reader audit the treatment variable directly and reconstruct it without access to the underlying policy dataset, which is unusual and commendable for this literature.
- Table 3 gives the exact CIP two-digit codes behind every field grouping, so the outcome taxonomy is unambiguous at the CIP-2 level and can be rebuilt from IPEDS without guessing.
- The covariate list is enumerated item by item (in-state tuition and fees, grant aid per student, percent receiving aid, state and local appropriations per FTE, instructional expenditure per FTE, FTE enrollment, state per-capita income, unemployment, population by race/ethnicity), with the log transformation and 2021-CPI inflation adjustment stated.
- The estimator is named specifically enough to install: Sun and Abraham (2021) via Stata's eventstudyinteract for the main results, Gardner (2022) two-stage via did2s for a robustness check, plus conventional TWFE. Fixed effects (institution, year) and state-level clustering are stated consistently in the text and repeated in every figure note.
- Sample-restriction decisions are disclosed rather than buried: footnote 3 names the exact states dropped for pre-period PBF (6 states/79 institutions in the 4-year sample; 5 states/109 in the 2-year sample), footnote 2 names the 64 mixed baccalaureate/associate colleges, and footnote 4 explains the collapsing of IPEDS' two long-certificate categories.
- Descriptive Tables 4–7 report base-year means and SDs for every outcome and covariate separately by treatment arm, which gives a replicator a set of checkable targets to hit before running any regression.

**Weaknesses:**

- No numeric results are reported anywhere. Every finding lives in Figures 1–5, each of which crams 6–8 field panels x 2 student populations x 3 overlaid treatment series x 11 event times into a page. There is no results table, no appendix table of coefficients, and no reported N per regression. For a paper whose entire claim is a null, this is disqualifying for verification: readers cannot distinguish a precisely estimated zero from an uninformative one for any specific field, credential, or subgroup.
- No data availability statement and no replication package. The article ends with COI, funding (Arnold Ventures 23-09389), and ORCID sections — exactly where a DAS would sit — and there is none. No code is posted, and there is not even an 'available on request' line.
- The InformEd States PBF dataset reference (Ortagus, Rosinger, & Kelchen, 2021) carries no URL, DOI, version, or vintage. Since this dataset supplies the treatment variable, and PBF coding decisions (what counts as 'funded,' how dosage shares are measured) are exactly where two coders would disagree, its access pathway should have been documented. Tables 1–2 partially compensate, but the 10% dosage threshold cannot be audited at all: the underlying share-of-funding figures are never shown for any state-year.
- The stated sample counts do not reconcile. The text says the sample includes 446 four-year and 807 two-year institutions, then says '27 states (446 institutions) adopted PBF' in the 4-year sector — 446 cannot be both the full sample and the treated subsample. Table 4's Ns are 185 (no PBF) + 248 (any PBF) = 433, not 446. In the 2-year sector, the text says 626 institutions adopted PBF, but Table 5 reports 614; and 168 + 614 = 782, not 807. A replicator has no way to know which count corresponds to the estimation sample.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** Partly withdrawn. Every table note says the descriptive statistics are for the base year (2003), and institutions in the 2003–2020 panel that are absent from the base year account for the gaps: 446 − 433 = 13 four-year institutions, and 807 − 782 = 25 two-year (12 of the 626 adopters and 13 of the 181 comparison institutions). The working paper's pre-exclusion 526/916 minus footnote 3's removals gives 447/807. So 446, 807 and 626 are consistent with the tables as panel totals, though the article never says so, and the MDE calculation, which uses the totals, is unaffected. What does not reconcile is p. 7's "27 states (446 institutions) adopted PBF": 446 is the whole four-year sample, and with 185 never-adopters in Table 4 the treated count must lie between 248 and 261. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered tables and the working paper.

- Handling of zeros in the logged count outcomes is never stated. The outcomes are ln(number of completions) by CIP-2 field, race subgroup, and credential; Table 5 shows means as low as 2.5 RM associate degrees in engineering, so structural zeros are pervasive, especially in the RM panels and small subfields. Whether the authors used ln(y), ln(y+1), IHS, or dropped zero cells is unreported, and each choice changes both the estimates and the effective sample. This is the single largest undocumented step in rebuilding the analytic dataset.
- Treatment is non-absorbing but the cohort definition is never given. Tables 1 and 2 show states switching PBF on and off (Kansas 4-year: 2006–2009, 2013, 2015, 2019–2020; Kansas 2-year high-dosage: 2006, 2008, 2020; Florida 4-year: 2008, then 2013–2020; Minnesota, Oregon, Massachusetts similar). The Sun–Abraham interaction-weighted estimator requires an absorbing first-treatment cohort variable. How event time was assigned for on/off states — first-ever adoption, longest spell, re-entry as a new cohort — is not stated, and it is decisive for what the figures show. The same problem arises for workforce and high-dosage PBF, whose start years often postdate the 'any PBF' start year in the same state.
- Equation 1 is not the estimated model. As printed on p. 10 it is a plain TWFE event study, sum over k = -5 to 5, k != -1, with no cohort interactions; the figure notes then say the plotted coefficients are 'beta^k in Equation 1 produced by the event study estimator developed by Sun and Abraham (2021).' The SA estimand is an interaction-weighted aggregation of cohort-specific effects, not beta^k of that equation. The indexing inside the equation is also inconsistent with the prose: PBF_{i,t+k} is described as equaling 1 if the institution 'adopted PBF k years before t.' Whether the endpoints are binned is not stated, yet the associate-degree discussion refers to estimates '5 years and beyond' when the plotted window ends at 5.
- The minimum detectable effect calculation is both unverifiable and internally inconsistent with the models it is meant to characterize. The formula (z_{alpha/2} + z_beta) x SE is given, but the SE input is not. Backing it out: at alpha = .0028 and 80% power the multiplier is 3.83, so a 9% MDE implies SE = 0.024; at alpha = .0015 the multiplier is 4.02, so an 11% MDE implies SE = 0.027. The authors state these come from 'robust standard errors at the institution level' — but every reported regression clusters at the state level (roughly 30–50 clusters), which will produce standard errors several times larger. The whiskers in Figures 1–3, drawn at ~3 SE, are visibly far wider than the ~0.07–0.09 half-widths those implied SEs would produce. The power claim therefore does not describe the models actually estimated, and readers cannot recompute it.
- The Bonferroni divisor is never derived. alpha = .0028 implies 18 hypotheses and alpha = .0015 implies 33, but the actual number of estimated coefficients runs into the hundreds (8 fields x 3 treatments x 2 populations x 11 event times in Figure 1 alone). Which family the correction is over is unstated and therefore not reproducible. Relatedly, the Figure 2 and 3 notes state that alpha = .0015 corresponds to '99.99% CIs'; 1 - .0015 = 99.85%, so the reported CI level is wrong on its face and a replicator matching interval widths would be misled.
- Institution-level treatment carve-outs inside state-years are described in prose only and cannot be coded reliably. Table 1's note excludes 'UMass institutions,' the University of Vermont, and Kentucky State University in 2018, and restricts Minnesota to University of Minnesota and MnSCU institutions with 'MnSCU institutions only in 2018 to 2019.' Table 2's note restricts South Carolina to technical colleges and Wisconsin to WTCS institutions 'in 2015 to 2018' — while the Table 2 cell for Wisconsin reads '2015–2020 (WTCS),' an outright inconsistency. No IPEDS UnitIDs or system crosswalk is provided for any of these.
- The 2021 Carnegie classification is applied retroactively across a 2003–2020 panel. This silently drops institutions that closed or merged before 2021, misclassifies institutions that changed level mid-panel, and creates a version dependency (which Carnegie file, which variable — Basic 2021?) that is never pinned down.
- IPEDS Completions construction details are omitted: first-major only versus first-and-second-major, which award-level codes map to 'certificate' short and long, whether the CIP revisions across 2000/2010/2020 vintages were harmonized over the 18-year panel, and how 'fiscal year 2003 to 2020' maps onto IPEDS completion survey years. The Census series used for state population by race and per-capita income is not named either.
- Thirty-six supplemental appendix figures (A1–A36) carry a large share of the paper's inferential weight — the claim that the one apparent effect (high-dosage PBF on health completions at doctoral universities) is 'not supported by estimates derived from alternative specifications' rests entirely on Figures A4, A9, and A14 — yet the text contains no supplemental-material statement, link, or DOI telling readers where to find them, and no description of their contents beyond a figure-number range.
- No software environment is reported: no Stata version, no package versions for eventstudyinteract or did2s (both of which have changed behavior across releases), and no data vintage or download date for IPEDS.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Treat every specific null in this paper as directionally suggestive but quantitatively unverifiable. Because no coefficients, standard errors, or CI bounds are printed, you cannot tell from the article whether 'no effect on STEM bachelor's completion' means a tight zero or an interval spanning economically large effects in both directions. If you need to cite a magnitude or a bound, request the underlying estimates from the corresponding author before doing so.
- Do not rely on the reported MDEs of 9% and 11% as the paper's power. Recompute them: the multiplier at alpha = .0028 with 80% power is 3.83, implying an input SE of 0.024, while the models actually reported cluster at the state level. Compare the whisker half-widths in Figures 1–3 against 3 x 0.024 = 0.07 on the plotted log scale; they are visibly much wider. The honest statement of precision for these estimates is the CI widths in the figures, not the stated MDE — and for the high-dosage arm (69 four-year institutions in Table 4), those are wide enough that the null is close to uninformative.
- If you want to reproduce this study, the treatment variable is the easy part and the outcome variable is the hard part. Tables 1 and 2 give you the full state-year policy coding directly; you can build 'any PBF,' 'workforce PBF,' and 'high-dosage PBF' from the printed tables without the InformEd States file. Budget your effort instead for the IPEDS Completions extract, where you must independently choose first-major versus all-major counts, award-level to certificate-length mapping, CIP-vintage harmonization across 2003–2020, and — critically — a zero-handling rule for the logged counts. Run the analysis under ln(y+1), IHS, and drop-zeros and report how much the RM and small-field results move; that sensitivity is the most likely source of divergence from the published figures.
- Ask the authors directly for four things before treating the results as settled: (1) the coefficient/SE/N tables underlying Figures 1–5 and A1–A36; (2) the cohort-assignment rule used for eventstudyinteract given that treatment turns on and off in Kansas, Florida, Minnesota, Oregon, Massachusetts and others, and how event time is set for workforce and high-dosage treatments that begin after 'any PBF' in the same state; (3) the zero-handling rule for the logged outcomes; (4) the IPEDS UnitID lists implementing the Table 1/Table 2 note-level carve-outs (UMass, University of Vermont, Kentucky State 2018, University of Minnesota/MnSCU, SC technical colleges, WTCS).
- Reconcile the sample counts before using any N from this paper. The text's 446 four-year institutions conflicts with Table 4 (185 + 248 = 433) and with the claim that 446 institutions are the PBF-adopting group; the 2-year text figure of 626 adopters conflicts with Table 5's 614, and 168 + 614 = 782 against a stated 807. Note also that Table 1 counts South Carolina among the 27 four-year adopting states on the strength of a 1998–2002 PBF spell that lies entirely outside the 2003–2020 window, and that New Jersey and Vermont enter only in 2020, contributing at most k = 0.
- Do not lean on the robustness claims without seeing the supplemental appendix. The paper's disposal of its one apparent positive result (high-dosage PBF on health completions at doctoral universities) rests wholly on Figures A4, A9, and A14, which are neither described nor linked in the text. Retrieve the supplemental file from the Sage article page and confirm those three figures actually show what the sentence asserts before citing the null as robust.
- Check the reported CI levels yourself: the notes to Figures 2 and 3 say alpha = .0015 corresponds to '99.99% CIs' when it corresponds to 99.85%. If you are trying to reverse-engineer standard errors from whisker lengths, use 3.18 SE (the correct z for .0015 two-sided), not the level printed in the note.
- Do not treat the 'high-dosage' variable as independently auditable. Unlike 'any PBF' and 'workforce PBF,' whose years are printed, the 10% funding-share threshold depends on state-year dosage estimates that appear nowhere in the article. Any replication of the high-dosage results is effectively conditional on obtaining the InformEd States dosage series from the authors and accepting their coding of it.
- For the purposes of citing this paper, the safest use is as evidence that field-targeted and high-dosage PBF designs did not produce large, robust completion gains through 2020 — the pattern across many outcomes and estimators is consistent, and that pattern-level conclusion survives the reporting gaps. The unsafe uses are citing precision, citing a specific field-by-subgroup null, or citing the reported power to rule out modest effects; none of those is checkable as published.

**Detailed Commentary:**

Verification profile of this paper. The data layer is the strongest part. Nothing here is restricted-use: IPEDS Completions and institutional characteristics/finance are freely downloadable, Census state population and income series are public, and the InformEd States PBF policy data are effectively reproduced inside the article itself in Tables 1 and 2. Publishing the full state-by-year treatment matrix — separately for the 4-year and 2-year sectors, and separately for the workforce-premium and high-dosage variants — is more than most papers in this literature do, and it means the treatment variable is auditable line by line. The main gap on this layer is the dosage series behind the 10% threshold, which is never shown for any state-year and cannot be checked at all, and the fact that the dataset citation carries no URL, DOI, or version.

The analytic-dataset layer has one gap large enough to block replication on its own. The outcomes are logs of completion counts disaggregated by CIP-2 field, credential type, certificate length, and RM subgroup. In the 2-year RM panels, base-year means run to 2.5 (engineering associate degrees) and 2.9 (engineering certificates); at that scale a large fraction of institution-year cells are zero. The paper never says what happens to those cells. ln(y), ln(y+1), IHS, and dropping zeros give materially different point estimates and different effective samples, and there is no way to infer the choice from anything reported. Alongside this sit a set of smaller but real ambiguities: first-major versus all-major IPEDS counts, the award-level codes mapping to short and long certificates, whether CIP vintages were harmonized over 2003–2020, and how 'fiscal year' aligns with IPEDS survey years. The 2021 Carnegie classification applied retroactively over an 18-year panel is a further silent restriction — institutions that closed or merged before 2021 simply are not in the frame.

The specification layer is described in more detail than average but does not survive close reading. Equation 1 as printed is a standard TWFE event study over k = -5 to 5 with k = -1 omitted, yet the figure notes attribute the plotted coefficients to the Sun–Abraham estimator, whose estimand is an interaction-weighted aggregation of cohort-specific effects rather than beta^k of that equation. More seriously, Sun–Abraham requires an absorbing cohort variable, and Tables 1 and 2 make clear that treatment is not absorbing: Kansas 4-year is on in 2006–2009, 2013, 2015, and 2019–2020; Kansas 2-year is high-dosage in 2006, 2008, and 2020 alone; Florida, Minnesota, Oregon, Massachusetts, and Michigan all show gaps. The paper acknowledges the mixture of maintainers and abandoners in one sentence but never states the rule that converts these on/off histories into an event-time index, nor how event time is set for workforce and high-dosage treatments that begin years after 'any PBF' in the same state. Two replicators following the text would produce different figures.

The inference layer contains an arithmetic inconsistency a reader can check without any data. The MDE formula is given as (z_{alpha/2} + z_beta) x SE. At alpha = .0028 with 80% power the multiplier is 3.831, so the claimed 9% MDE implies an input SE of 0.024; at alpha = .0015 the multiplier is 4.016, so the claimed 11% implies 0.027. The authors say plainly that these come from institution-level robust standard errors, while every model reported clusters on state with roughly 30–50 clusters. The CI whiskers in Figures 1–3, drawn at roughly 3 SE under the stated alphas, span a large share of a y-axis running about -0.8 to 0.8 — far more than the 0.07–0.09 half-widths the MDE inputs would generate. The reported power therefore characterizes a model the paper does not estimate, and the honest read is that these nulls are considerably less precise than the MDE section implies, particularly for high-dosage PBF, which rests on 69 four-year institutions. In the same vein, the Bonferroni divisors (18 and 33 hypotheses implied by alpha = .0028 and .0015) are never derived and sit far below the several hundred coefficients actually plotted, and the Figure 2/3 notes misstate the CI level as 99.99% when .0015 corresponds to 99.85%.

The results layer is where verification fails outright. The article reports no point estimate, no standard error, no confidence bound, and no per-regression sample size — not in the text, not in a table, not in a note. Everything is compressed into five figures of 12–16 miniature panels apiece with three overlaid treatment series, at a resolution where individual coefficients cannot be read. Thirty-six additional supplemental figures carry the robustness argument, including the specific figures (A4, A9, A14) invoked to dismiss the single apparent positive effect in the paper, yet no supplemental-material statement, link, or description appears anywhere in the article. For a paper whose contribution is a null result across many designs, this is the wrong reporting choice: a null is only informative in proportion to its precision, and precision is exactly what has been withheld.

Internal consistency is imperfect in ways that compound the above. The 4-year sample is stated as 446 institutions and, two paragraphs later, 446 is also given as the number of institutions in the 27 PBF-adopting states; Table 4 sums to 433. The 2-year text reports 626 adopting institutions against Table 5's 614, and Table 5 sums to 782 against a stated 807. Table 1 counts South Carolina among the adopting states on the basis of a 1998–2002 spell entirely outside the analytic window. Table 2's Wisconsin cell reads 2015–2020 while its own note restricts WTCS institutions to 2015–2018. The institution-level carve-outs in both table notes (UMass, University of Vermont, Kentucky State in 2018, University of Minnesota/MnSCU, South Carolina technical colleges) are described in prose without UnitIDs or a system crosswalk, so they cannot be implemented deterministically.

Net assessment for readers. Roughly the treatment side of this study is independently checkable and the outcome, estimation, and inference sides are not. A skilled replicator with public IPEDS data and Tables 1–2 could rebuild something close to the design, but would have to guess on zero-handling, cohort assignment under non-absorbing treatment, IPEDS award-level and major-count conventions, and the Carnegie vintage — and, having done so, would have no published numbers to check the reconstruction against. The paper's broad conclusion (field-targeted and high-dosage PBF did not produce large robust completion gains through 2020) is consistent across many cuts and is a reasonable thing to cite at that altitude. Any narrower claim — a specific field, a specific subgroup, a bound on how small an effect can be ruled out — should be treated as unverified until the authors release estimates and code. Rated weak rather than insufficient because the data are public, the policy coding is fully printed, and the design is describable; rated weak rather than adequate because a 2026 journal article with no data availability statement, no replication package, and zero reported numbers offers readers no way to check the central results.
